questions.title: What is the difference between blocking (=) and nonblocking (<=) assignments?
questions.answer: Blocking (=) for combinational/sequential calculations within a block; nonblocking (<=) for clocked logic so all RHS are sampled before updates. Mixing them carelessly creates races.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Blocking `=` updates the LHS immediately so later statements see the new value (use it for combinational logic); nonblocking `<=` samples every RHS first and updates all LHS together in the NBA region (use it for clocked logic).

```systemverilog
// shift register: q1 <= d; q2 <= q1;  -> 2 flops
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  q1 <= d;
  q2 <= q1;     // sees OLD q1
end

// same code with '=' -> q2 = d after one clock (1 flop collapsed)
always @(posedge clk) begin
  q1 = d;
  q2 = q1;      // sees NEW q1 == d
end
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p....."}, {"name": "d", "wave": "0.1..."}, {"name": "q1 (<=)", "wave": "0..1.."}, {"name": "q2 (<=)", "wave": "0...1."}, {"name": "q2 (=)", "wave": "0..1.."}], "head": {"text": "nonblocking gives a 2-stage pipeline; blocking collapses it"}}
```

### Explanation
- Blocking: executes and updates in the Active region, in statement order.
- Nonblocking: RHS evaluated in Active, LHS update scheduled in the NBA region after all Active events at this time step.
- Guideline (Cummings): `<=` in `always_ff`, `=` in `always_comb`, never mix both on the same variable.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Blocking in clocked blocks causes read/write races between different `always` blocks.
- Mixing `=` and `<=` to the same variable is a lint error and a synthesis/simulation mismatch risk.

### Follow-ups
- *Can you use `=` for a temp variable inside `always_ff`?* Yes if it is local and only used in that block, but many coding standards forbid it.
- *What does `#0` do?* Moves the process to the Inactive region; it is a hack, not a fix for races.

questions.title: Why are nonblocking assignments preferred in sequential logic?
questions.answer: NBAs evaluate RHS at the clock event and update LHS later in the NBA region, so all registers see the same old state, like real parallel hardware.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A nonblocking assignment models a flip-flop: every register samples its D input at the clock edge (old values) and all outputs change together afterwards, independent of the order of `always` blocks.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E["posedge clk"] --> ACT["Active region: evaluate all RHS (old values)"]
  ACT --> NBA["NBA region: update all LHS together"]
  NBA --> COMB["combinational logic re-evaluates (new deltas)"]
```

```systemverilog
// order-independent swap: works only with <=
always_ff @(posedge clk) a <= b;
always_ff @(posedge clk) b <= a;
```

### Explanation
- Real flops all capture at the same edge; nonblocking reproduces that because LHS updates are deferred to the NBA region.
- With blocking, whichever `always` block the simulator runs first would overwrite a value that another block still needs to read -> race.
- The swap example above exchanges `a` and `b` each clock regardless of scheduling order.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Nonblocking does not fix a race when the *reader* is in a testbench sampling with blocking code at the same edge; use clocking blocks or sample on the opposite edge.

### Follow-ups
- *Is the NBA region after Inactive?* Yes: Active -> Inactive (#0) -> NBA; NBA updates can trigger new Active events (another delta).

questions.title: What is a race condition in Verilog, and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer: Result depends on simulator scheduling order; common with blocking writes/reads of shared variables in multiple always blocks. Use NBAs, single writer, clocking blocks.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A race exists when the result depends on the order in which the simulator executes concurrent processes scheduled at the same time step; the IEEE standard leaves that order undefined.

```systemverilog
// RACE: both blocks triggered by the same edge, blocking assignments
always @(posedge clk) a = b;
always @(posedge clk) c = a;   // c gets old or new a depending on order

// FIX
always_ff @(posedge clk) a <= b;
always_ff @(posedge clk) c <= a;   // always old a
```

| Race type | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Two always blocks, blocking write/read of same var | Use `<=` for clocked logic |
| Testbench drives DUT input at the clock edge | Clocking block with output skew, or drive on negedge / with `<=` |
| Multiple drivers to one variable | Single-writer rule (`always_ff`/`always_comb` enforce it) |
| `initial` vs `always` at time 0 | Avoid relying on time-0 ordering; use reset |

### Explanation
- Read-write race: one process writes, another reads at the same time step.
- Write-write race: two processes write; last one wins arbitrarily.
- Different simulators (or even different compile options) can give different results, so races are real bugs even if a test passes.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `#0` delays only shift the problem; they are not a robust fix.

### Follow-ups
- *How does a clocking block avoid TB races?* It samples inputs in the Preponed region (before the edge) and drives outputs after the edge with skew, so TB and DUT never update at the same instant.

questions.title: Explain the Verilog/SystemVerilog event scheduling regions.
questions.answer: Regions: active, inactive, NBA, observed, reactive, postponed (plus preponed, re-inactive, re-NBA in SV). Explains #0, <=, assertions, clocking blocks.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Each time step is split into ordered regions; knowing them explains why `<=`, `#0`, assertions and clocking blocks behave differently. Main order: Preponed -> Active -> Inactive -> NBA -> Observed -> Reactive -> Re-Inactive -> Re-NBA -> Postponed.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  PRE["Preponed: sample values for assertions / clocking block inputs"] --> ACT["Active: module code, blocking =, RHS of <=, continuous assign"]
  ACT --> INA["Inactive: #0 processes"]
  INA --> NBA["NBA: update LHS of <="]
  NBA -->|new events| ACT
  NBA --> OBS["Observed: evaluate concurrent assertions"]
  OBS --> REA["Reactive: program blocks, assertion action blocks, TB code"]
  REA --> RIN["Re-Inactive / Re-NBA"]
  RIN -->|new events| ACT
  RIN --> POST["Postponed: $strobe, $monitor (final values)"]
```

| Construct | Region |
| --- | --- |
| `a = b` / RHS of `a <= b` | Active |
| `#0` | Inactive |
| LHS update of `<=` | NBA |
| concurrent assertion evaluation | Observed (values sampled in Preponed) |
| program block code, clocking-block drives | Reactive / Re-NBA |
| `$strobe`, `$monitor` | Postponed |

### Explanation
- The Active set (Active, Inactive, NBA) is for design code; the Reactive set (Reactive, Re-Inactive, Re-NBA) is for testbench code, so the TB sees settled design values.
- Assertions use values from the Preponed region, i.e. the values *before* the clock edge.
- `$display` prints in Active (may show pre-NBA values); `$strobe` prints in Postponed (settled values).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Within a region, process order is undefined; never depend on it.

### Follow-ups
- *Why does `$display` after `a <= 1` show the old value?* The NBA update has not happened yet.
- *Where do SVA action blocks run?* Reactive region.

questions.title: What is a delta cycle?
questions.answer: Zero-time simulation step to propagate events between processes without advancing time; combinational chains and NBA updates may need several.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A delta cycle is a zero-time iteration of the scheduler: events propagate through processes and NBA updates without advancing simulation time, until no more events are pending at that time step.

| Delta | Event at t = 10 ns |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | posedge clk -> `q <= d` scheduled |
| 1 | NBA: q updates |
| 2 | `assign n = ~q` re-evaluates |
| 3 | `always_comb y = n & en` re-evaluates |
| 4 | no more events -> time advances |

```systemverilog
assign n = ~q;          // delta after q changes
always_comb y = n & en; // another delta
always_ff @(posedge clk) q <= d;
```

### Explanation
- Simulation time stays at 10 ns while the chain settles; waveform viewers show only the final value (some can expand deltas).
- Zero-delay combinational loops create infinite deltas -> the simulator hangs or reports an iteration limit.
- Delta glitches can trigger `always @(x)` blocks multiple times in one time step.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Clock gating/derived clocks with zero-delay assigns can make a derived clock edge happen one delta later than data, creating a simulation race (data captured with new value).

### Follow-ups
- *How to see deltas?* Many simulators support delta-expanded waveforms (e.g. `-deltacycle` in some tools).

questions.title: always_comb vs always @* — what are the differences?
questions.answer: always_comb: auto sensitivity, runs at time 0, forbids multiple drivers; always @* is older syntax without these checks.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Both model combinational logic, but `always_comb` adds semantic checks: it runs once at time zero, is sensitive to variables read in called functions, and forbids other processes from writing its outputs.

| Feature | always @* | always_comb |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executes at time 0 | No (waits for an event) | Yes, once after all initial/always start |
| Sensitive to vars read inside called functions | No (only args) | Yes |
| Multiple drivers of the LHS allowed | Yes | No (compile error) |
| Timing controls (#, @) inside | Allowed | Illegal |
| Tool checks for latch inference | No | Lint/synthesis warn if latch inferred |

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  y = '0;                 // default avoids latch
  if (sel) y = a;
end
```

### Explanation
- The time-0 execution fixes the classic bug where an `always @*` output stays X until an input changes.
- Expressing intent lets lint/synthesis flag latches that slipped into a combinational block.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `always_comb` is not sensitive to its own LHS or to variables written inside it, so it cannot model intended combinational loops.

### Follow-ups
- *What about `always_latch`?* Same rules but declares intended latch storage.

questions.title: always_ff vs always @(posedge clk) — what does always_ff add?
questions.answer: always_ff communicates sequential intent and lets tools check event controls and drivers; hardware is still decided by the sensitivity and assignments.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `always_ff` declares intent to model sequential logic: tools check it has exactly one event control, no blocking timing controls, and that its variables are not written by other processes. It does not by itself create a flop; the edge-sensitive event and assignments do.

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) q <= '0;
  else        q <= d;

// errors/warnings tools give inside always_ff:
//   #5 q <= d;          -> timing control not allowed
//   another always writes q -> multiple driver error
```

| Check | always @(posedge clk) | always_ff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One event control at the top only | not enforced | enforced |
| Other process writes same var | allowed | error |
| Intent visible to lint/synthesis | no | yes (warns if no flop inferred) |

### Explanation
- Use `always_ff` for flops, `always_comb` for logic, `always_latch` for latches; mixing intent in one block is avoided.
- Use `<=` inside `always_ff`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Writing `always_ff @(clk)` (level) is legal syntax but synthesis will error/warn because no edge flop can be inferred.

### Follow-ups
- *Can `always_ff` have an async reset?* Yes: `@(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)` with the reset tested first.

questions.title: What is always_latch, and when is a latch inferred?
questions.answer: always_latch expresses intended level-sensitive storage; latches are inferred when a combinational process doesn't assign its output on every path.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `always_latch` declares intentional level-sensitive storage. A latch is inferred whenever a combinational process leaves an output unassigned on some path, so it must hold its previous value.

```systemverilog
always_latch
  if (en) q = d;        // transparent while en=1, holds while en=0
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "en", "wave": "0.1..0..1.0."}, {"name": "d", "wave": "=.=.=.=.=.=.", "data": ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]}, {"name": "q", "wave": "x.=.==..==..", "data": ["b", "c", "c", "e", "e"]}], "head": {"text": "latch: q follows d while en=1, holds when en falls"}}
```

### Explanation
- `always_latch` = intent; tools warn if the block does *not* infer a latch.
- In `always_comb`, a missing `else` or `default` creates an unintended latch and tools warn.
- Latches are level-sensitive, so timing analysis uses time borrowing; most ASIC flows avoid them except in clock gating cells.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A latch-based design is hard to verify for glitches on the enable; keep enables glitch-free (e.g. driven from flops).

### Follow-ups
- *Why does an ICG cell contain a latch?* To hold the enable stable while the clock is high so the gated clock does not glitch.

questions.title: What causes unintended latch inference, and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: Variable not assigned on every path in a combinational process -> storage required. Fix with defaults at the start or covering all branches.

questions.title: wire vs reg vs logic — what is the difference?
questions.answer: wire = net driven continuously; reg = procedural variable (not necessarily a flop); logic = 4-state variable replacing reg, single driver; use nets for multi-driver.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `wire` is a net (resolved, multi-driver capable, driven by `assign`/ports); `reg` is a Verilog variable written procedurally (not necessarily a flop); `logic` is SystemVerilog's 4-state variable that can be driven by one continuous assign *or* procedural code, replacing `reg`.

| Type | Kind | Driven by | Multiple drivers | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wire | net | assign, port, gate | yes (resolved) | connections, tri-state buses |
| reg | variable | procedural block | no resolution | legacy Verilog procedural outputs |
| logic | variable (4-state) | one assign OR procedural | no (error) | default SV type |
| bit | variable (2-state) | procedural | no | TB, counters |

```systemverilog
logic y, z;
assign y = a & b;          // legal: single continuous driver
always_comb z = c | d;     // legal: procedural driver
// assign z = e;           // ERROR: z already driven procedurally
wire bus; assign bus = en1 ? d1 : 'z; assign bus = en2 ? d2 : 'z; // multi-driver net
```

### Explanation
- `reg` does not imply a register; `always @*` with `reg` gives combinational logic.
- Use `logic` everywhere except where a resolved multi-driver net (bidirectional/tri-state) is needed; then use `wire`/`tri`.
- `logic` catches accidental multiple drivers at compile time.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Ports declared `inout` must be nets.

### Follow-ups
- *What is `wire logic`?* A net with 4-state logic datatype; `logic` alone defaults to a variable.

questions.title: Explain 4-state logic values 0, 1, X, Z.
questions.answer: 4-state models 0,1,X,Z. X exposes uninitialized/conflicting signals; hardware is binary so X/Z need careful interpretation.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** 4-state types (`logic`, `reg`, `wire`, `integer`) hold 0, 1, X (unknown/conflict) and Z (high impedance). X exposes uninitialized or contended signals in simulation; real silicon only has 0/1, so X/Z must be interpreted as 'could be either'.

| Value | Meaning | Typical source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 / 1 | logic low / high | normal drive |
| X | unknown | uninitialized flop, 0/1 contention, X-propagation |
| Z | not driven | tri-state disabled, floating input |

| a & b | 0 | 1 | X | Z |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | X | X |
| X | 0 | X | X | X |
| Z | 0 | X | X | X |

### Explanation
- 2-state types (`bit`, `int`, `byte`) convert X/Z to 0, which hides bugs but simulates faster.
- X-optimism: `if (x_sig)` takes the else branch, hiding an X; X-pessimism: gate-level sims may propagate X where silicon would be fine.
- Use assertions like `assert property (@(posedge clk) !$isunknown(data))` on critical signals.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Assigning a 4-state X into a 2-state `bit` silently becomes 0.

### Follow-ups
- *How does a Z on a gate input behave?* Treated as X by logic operators.

questions.title: What is the difference between == and ===?
questions.answer: == is logical equality and may return X; === is case equality comparing X/Z literally, always 0/1. Use === in verification.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `==` is logical equality and returns X if any compared bit is X/Z; `===` is case equality, compares X and Z literally and always returns 0 or 1.

| Expression | == | === |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4'b1010 vs 4'b1010 | 1 | 1 |
| 4'b10x0 vs 4'b1010 | x | 0 |
| 4'b10x0 vs 4'b10x0 | x | 1 |
| 4'b0x00 vs 4'b1x00 | 0 (a known bit differs) | 0 |
| 1'bz vs 1'bz | x | 1 |

```systemverilog
if (data == 8'h55)  ...   // X in data -> condition is X -> treated false
if (data === 'x)    ...   // detect unknowns exactly
assert (!$isunknown(data)); // preferred X check
```

### Explanation
- `==`/`!=` propagate uncertainty (synthesizable).
- `===`/`!==` are for testbenches/checks and are not synthesizable in general.
- `==?` / `!=?` treat X/Z in the right operand as wildcards.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `if (a == b)` with X silently goes to `else`, hiding the X; prefer explicit `$isunknown` checks.

### Follow-ups
- *What does `inside` use?* `==?`-like wildcard semantics for set membership.

questions.title: == vs inside vs case equality: which do you use in verification checks?
questions.answer: Case equality for exact 4-state checks; == when X should propagate; inside for set membership with wildcard matching.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Use `===` for exact 4-state checks (an X is a mismatch), `==` when uncertainty should propagate, `==?` / `inside` for wildcard or set membership, and `$isunknown` to flag X explicitly.

| Operator | X/Z in DUT value | X/Z in pattern | Result type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `==` | -> X | -> X | 0/1/X |
| `===` | compared literally | compared literally | 0/1 |
| `==?` | -> X if it matters | wildcard | 0/1/X |
| `inside {...}` | uses `==?` semantics per item | wildcard | 0/1/X |

```systemverilog
bit ok;
ok = (actual === expected);             // strict scoreboard compare
if (opcode inside {[8'h10:8'h1F], 8'h80}) ...   // ranges + values
if (addr ==? 32'h0000_00??) ...         // ? = don't care in pattern
constraint c { mode inside {READ, WRITE}; }
```

### Explanation
- Scoreboards should use `===` (or `!==`) so an X from the DUT fails the compare instead of evaluating false silently.
- `inside` is the natural way to express sets in constraints and coverage-like checks.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `inside` returns X when the DUT value has X bits that matter; wrap with `$isunknown` if you need an error.

### Follow-ups
- *Is `inside` synthesizable?* Yes for constant sets; tools convert it to comparators.

questions.title: case vs casez vs casex — which should you use?
questions.answer: case exact 4-state; casez Z/? as don't care; casex X and Z as don't care (hides X bugs, discouraged).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `case` matches all 4 states exactly; `casez` treats Z/`?` as don't care; `casex` treats both X and Z as don't care, which can hide X bugs, so prefer `casez` (or `case inside`) for wildcards.

| sel value | item 2'b1? | case | casez | casex |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2'b10 |  | no match | match | match |
| 2'b1x |  | no match | no match | match (X hidden!) |
| 2'bx0 |  | no match | no match | match item 2'bx? patterns |

```systemverilog
// priority encoder with casez
always_comb begin
  casez (req)
    4'b1???: gnt = 2'd3;
    4'b01??: gnt = 2'd2;
    4'b001?: gnt = 2'd1;
    default: gnt = 2'd0;
  endcase
end
// SV alternative: case (req) inside 4'b1???: ... endcase
```

### Explanation
- `casex`: an X on the selector matches any item, so the sim picks a branch while silicon is unknown -> sim/synth mismatch.
- `case ... inside` (SV) uses `==?` semantics with wildcards only in the items, not the selector: safest.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- With `casez`, a Z on the selector still matches; lint for Z on selects.

### Follow-ups
- *Synthesis view?* All three synthesize the same mux/priority logic; the difference is simulation semantics.

questions.title: What do unique case and priority case mean?
questions.answer: unique: at most one match and full coverage expected; priority: first match wins, missing coverage checked. Use only when assumptions are true.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `unique` asserts that at most one item matches and that some item always matches (parallel, full); `priority` asserts that the first match wins and some item always matches (full). Simulators report violations; synthesis may optimize based on them.

| Keyword | Overlap allowed | No-match allowed | Synthesis hint | Sim check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (none) | yes, first wins | yes | priority logic | none |
| unique | no | no (unless default) | parallel_case + full_case | warning on overlap or no match |
| unique0 | no | yes | parallel_case | warning on overlap |
| priority | yes, first wins | no (unless default) | full_case | warning on no match |

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  unique case (state)        // one-hot states never overlap
    IDLE: nxt = start ? RUN : IDLE;
    RUN : nxt = done  ? IDLE : RUN;
  endcase                    // runtime warning if state is neither
end
```

### Explanation
- They replace the dangerous synthesis pragmas `// synopsys full_case parallel_case`, but now simulation checks the claim.
- Use only when the assumption is true; otherwise synthesis builds logic that differs from what simulation tested.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A `default` branch makes `unique` 'full' automatically, but overlap is still checked.

### Follow-ups
- *`unique if`?* Same semantics for if/else-if chains.

questions.title: What pitfalls arise with signed vs unsigned arithmetic?
questions.answer: Unsigned operands zero-extend, signed sign-extend; mixed expressions become unsigned. Cast explicitly or declare consistently.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** If **any** operand in an expression is unsigned, the whole expression is evaluated unsigned and operands are zero-extended; only all-signed expressions sign-extend. Mixing them silently changes comparisons and extensions.

```systemverilog
logic signed [7:0] a = -8'sd1;   // 8'hFF
logic        [7:0] b = 8'd1;
logic signed [15:0] s;

s = a;                 // 16'hFFFF  (sign-extended)  = -1
s = a + b;             // b unsigned -> a treated unsigned: 255+1 = 256 = 16'h0100
s = a + $signed(b);    // -1 + 1 = 0
if (a < b) ...         // unsigned compare: 255 < 1 -> FALSE
if (a < $signed(b))... // -1 < 1 -> TRUE
```

| Expression | Evaluated as | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a + b | unsigned | 256 |
| a + $signed(b) | signed | 0 |
| a < b | unsigned | 0 |

### Explanation
- Signedness is determined by the operands, not by the LHS.
- Width is extended to the max of operands and LHS *before* evaluation (context-determined).
- Part-selects and concatenations are always unsigned even if the source is signed.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `a[7:0]` of a signed vector is unsigned; `{a}` is unsigned too.

### Follow-ups
- *Integer literal `-1` vs `'1`?* `-1` is a signed 32-bit int; `'1` fills all bits with 1 in context width.

questions.title: What are the pitfalls of unsized constants and expression widths?
questions.answer: Unsized decimal literals are int-sized and signed, affecting width/signedness; use explicitly sized literals for portable RTL.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** An unsized literal like `5` or `'hF` is at least 32 bits and signed (decimal); it widens the expression and can change results, e.g. overflow is preserved or comparisons become signed. Size literals explicitly when width matters.

```systemverilog
logic [3:0] a = 4'hF, b = 4'h1;
logic [4:0] sum;
sum = a + b;            // 5-bit context: 5'h10 (carry kept)
if (a + b == 0) ...     // 32-bit context because 0 is 32-bit: 16 != 0 -> FALSE
if (4'(a + b) == 4'd0)  // explicit 4-bit wrap -> TRUE

logic [63:0] big = 1 << 40;   // 1 is 32-bit: result 0 in some tools
logic [63:0] ok  = 64'd1 << 40;
```

| Literal | Width | Signed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | >= 32 | yes |
| 'd5 | >= 32 | no |
| 4'd5 | 4 | no |
| 4'sd5 | 4 | yes |
| '1 | context | no |

### Explanation
- Expression width = max(width of operands, LHS) for context-determined operators.
- Shifts: the left operand's width bounds the result before assignment context widening.
- Lint tools (e.g. width mismatch warnings) catch most issues.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Unsized hex constants wider than 32 bits are truncated/implementation-specific in Verilog-1995.

### Follow-ups
- *What is `'0`, `'1`, `'x`?* Fill literals that extend to the LHS width.

questions.title: What is implicit casting in SystemVerilog, and when should you use explicit casts?
questions.answer: Automatic conversion between types/sizes/signedness can hide truncation or sign extension; use $signed, $unsigned or typed casts.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** SV automatically converts between sizes, signedness and types on assignment and in expressions (truncate, zero/sign-extend, real<->int rounding). That is convenient but hides truncation and sign errors, so cast explicitly in critical arithmetic.

```systemverilog
logic [7:0]  b;
int          i = -3;
real         r = 2.7;
typedef enum {RED, GREEN} color_e;
color_e c;

b = i;                 // implicit: 8'hFD (truncated)
i = r;                 // implicit: rounds to 3
c = 1;                 // ILLEGAL: int -> enum needs a cast
c = color_e'(1);       // static cast (no check)
if (!$cast(c, 5)) $error("bad enum");   // dynamic cast with check
b = 8'(i);             // size cast
i = signed'(b);        // signedness cast  (or $signed(b))
```

| Cast | Checked at | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `T'(x)` | compile time (static) | size/sign/type conversions |
| `$cast(dst, src)` | run time | enum values, class downcasts |
| `$signed/$unsigned` | n/a | signedness only |

### Explanation
- Enums are strongly typed: assigning an int requires a cast.
- `$cast` returns 0 (or errors when called as a task) when the value is not legal, which is the safe choice for enums and class handles.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `real` to int conversion rounds (not truncates) to nearest.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you downcast a class handle?* `$cast(derived_h, base_h)`.

questions.title: Arithmetic (>>>) vs logical (>>) shift — what is the difference?
questions.answer: >> logical right shift fills zeros; >>> arithmetic right shift preserves sign for signed operands; left shifts fill zeros.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `>>` always fills with zeros; `>>>` fills with the sign bit **if the operand is signed**, implementing divide-by-2^n for negative numbers. Left shifts `<<` and `<<<` are identical (zero fill).

| Operand (8-bit) | >> 2 | >>> 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unsigned 8'b1001_0000 (144) | 0010_0100 (36) | 0010_0100 (36) |
| signed 8'sb1001_0000 (-112) | 0010_0100 (36) | 1110_0100 (-28) |

```systemverilog
logic signed [7:0] s = -8'sd112;
logic        [7:0] u = 8'd144;
$display("%0d %0d", s >>> 2, u >>> 2);   // -28 36
$display("%0d", $signed(u) >>> 2);       // -28 (cast makes it signed)
```

### Explanation
- Signedness of the *left operand* decides the fill for `>>>`.
- An arithmetic right shift of a negative number rounds toward minus infinity (-7 >>> 1 = -4), unlike `/ 2` which truncates toward zero (-3).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the expression is unsigned anywhere (e.g. part-select `s[7:0]`), `>>>` behaves like `>>`.

### Follow-ups
- *Synthesis?* Constant shifts are just wiring; variable shifts make a barrel shifter.

questions.title: What are reduction operators?
questions.answer: Reduction operators collapse a vector into one bit: & all-ones, | any-one, ^ parity; differ from bitwise operators.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Unary reduction operators (`& | ^ ~& ~| ~^`) collapse all bits of one vector into a single bit, unlike bitwise operators which combine two vectors bit by bit.

| Expression (v = 4'b1011) | Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| &v | 0 | all ones? |
| |v | 1 | any one? |
| ^v | 1 | odd parity |
| ~&v | 1 | NAND |
| ~|v | 0 | all zeros? |
| v & 4'b0110 | 4'b0010 | bitwise (vector) |

```systemverilog
assign all_ones = &data;          // e.g. counter == max
assign is_zero  = ~|data;         // zero detect
assign parity   = ^data;          // even-parity bit generator: data ^ parity -> even
assign has_x    = ^data === 1'bx; // quick X check
```

### Explanation
- Synthesis maps them to AND/OR/XOR trees, log2(N) levels deep.
- `^v === 1'bx` is a cheap way to detect any X/Z bit in a vector.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `!v` (logical NOT) equals `~|v`, but `~v` is a bitwise vector inverse — common confusion.

### Follow-ups
- *How to count ones?* `$countones(v)` in SV, or an adder tree in RTL.

questions.title: Continuous assignment vs procedural assignment — what is the difference?
questions.answer: Continuous assignment drives a net continuously; procedural assignments update variables when the process runs. Keep a single-driver discipline.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A continuous `assign` permanently drives a net (or SV variable) from an expression and re-evaluates whenever an operand changes; procedural assignments run only when their `initial`/`always` process executes and they update variables.

|  | Continuous (`assign`) | Procedural (`always`/`initial`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target | net, or variable with single driver (SV) | variable only |
| When evaluated | any RHS change | when the process is triggered |
| Control flow | expression only (`?:`) | if/case/loops |
| Multiple drivers | nets resolve; variables illegal | one process per variable (rule) |

```systemverilog
assign y = sel ? a : b;               // continuous mux
always_comb y2 = sel ? a : b;         // procedural equivalent
always_ff @(posedge clk) q <= y;      // procedural sequential
```

### Explanation
- Both forms can model combinational logic; choose `assign` for simple expressions and `always_comb` for multi-branch logic.
- SV allows `assign` to a `logic` variable, but then no procedural block may write it (single-driver discipline).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `assign` inside a procedural block (procedural continuous assign, `assign/deassign`, `force/release`) is a different, mostly testbench-only feature.

### Follow-ups
- *Delay in assign?* `assign #2 y = a;` models inertial delay (pulses shorter than 2 are filtered).

questions.title: parameter vs localparam — when do you use each?
questions.answer: parameter can be overridden at instantiation; localparam cannot and is for derived constants or fixed encodings.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `parameter` is a configurable constant that can be overridden at instantiation (`#(...)`) or via `defparam`; `localparam` cannot be overridden and is used for derived constants and internal encodings.

```systemverilog
module fifo #(
  parameter int DW    = 8,
  parameter int DEPTH = 16
) ( ... );
  localparam int AW = $clog2(DEPTH);      // derived - must stay consistent
  localparam logic [1:0] IDLE = 2'd0;     // internal encoding
  logic [AW:0] wptr, rptr;
endmodule

fifo #(.DW(32), .DEPTH(64)) u_fifo (...);  // override parameters only
```

|  | parameter | localparam |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Override at instantiation | yes | no |
| Can depend on other params | yes | yes |
| Typical use | width, depth, feature enable | derived widths, state encodings |

### Explanation
- Making derived values `localparam` prevents users from overriding them inconsistently (e.g. setting AW that doesn't match DEPTH).
- In SV packages and classes, `parameter` behaves like `localparam`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `defparam` is deprecated; use named parameter overrides.

### Follow-ups
- *Type parameters?* `parameter type T = logic [7:0]` lets you parameterize data types.

questions.title: What does $clog2 do, and what is its edge case?
questions.answer: $clog2 returns ceil(log2(N)); used for address/counter widths. $clog2(1)=0 can create zero-width declarations.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `$clog2(N)` returns ceil(log2(N)), the number of bits needed to index N items (0..N-1). Edge case: `$clog2(1) = 0`, which produces a zero-width `[-1:0]` vector.

| N | $clog2(N) | Address bits | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | zero width - guard it |
| 2 | 1 | 1 |  |
| 5 | 3 | 3 | not a power of 2 |
| 16 | 4 | 4 |  |
| 17 | 5 | 5 |  |

```systemverilog
localparam int AW = (DEPTH > 1) ? $clog2(DEPTH) : 1;   // guard DEPTH=1
logic [AW-1:0] addr;
// counter that must hold the value N itself (0..N): $clog2(N+1) bits
localparam int CW = $clog2(DEPTH + 1);
```

### Explanation
- To *count up to* N (inclusive) you need `$clog2(N+1)` bits; to *index* N entries you need `$clog2(N)`.
- Evaluated at elaboration time, so usable in parameter and port declarations.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Async FIFO pointers usually need `$clog2(DEPTH)+1` bits (extra wrap bit).

### Follow-ups
- *Before `$clog2` existed?* People wrote a constant function `clog2` in Verilog-2001.

questions.title: What are generate blocks used for?
questions.answer: Generate creates structure at elaboration time: parameterized arrays, optional features, repeated instances. Not a runtime loop.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Generate constructs (`for`, `if`, `case` generate) create hardware structure at elaboration time based on parameters: repeated instances, optional features, parameterized arrays. A generate loop is not a runtime loop.

```systemverilog
module adder_chain #(parameter int N = 4) (input logic [N-1:0] a, b, input logic ci,
                                          output logic [N-1:0] s, output logic co);
  logic [N:0] c;
  assign c[0] = ci;
  for (genvar i = 0; i < N; i++) begin : g_fa        // named block -> g_fa[0].u_fa
    full_adder u_fa (.a(a[i]), .b(b[i]), .ci(c[i]), .s(s[i]), .co(c[i+1]));
  end
  assign co = c[N];

  if (N > 8) begin : g_pipe     // conditional generate
    // insert a pipeline register for wide adders
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CI["ci"] --> FA0["g_fa[0]"] --> FA1["g_fa[1]"] --> FA2["g_fa[2]"] --> FA3["g_fa[3]"] --> CO["co"]
```

### Explanation
- Each iteration creates a named scope (`g_fa[i]`), useful for hierarchical references and debug.
- `genvar` exists only at elaboration.
- Generate `if`/`case` choose architecture by parameter (e.g. sync vs async reset, with/without ECC).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Always name generate blocks; unnamed ones get tool-specific names like `genblk1`.

### Follow-ups
- *Generate vs procedural for loop?* Generate replicates instances/continuous assigns; procedural for replicates logic inside a block.

questions.title: Is a for loop synthesizable, and what hardware does it create?
questions.answer: Synthesizable when bounds are static; unrolled into combinational/replicated logic, not sequential execution over clocks.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Yes, if its bounds are static (known at elaboration). Synthesis unrolls it into parallel/replicated logic in a single clock cycle; it does not execute iteratively over multiple clocks.

```systemverilog
// count ones: unrolls into an adder tree / chain
always_comb begin
  cnt = '0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++)
    cnt += data[i];
end

// bit reverse: pure wiring
always_comb
  for (int i = 0; i < W; i++) rev[i] = data[W-1-i];
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D0["data[0]"] --> A1["+"]
  D1["data[1]"] --> A1 --> A2["+"]
  D2["data[2]"] --> A2 --> A3["+ ... x8"]
  A3 --> CNT["cnt (one cycle)"]
```

### Explanation
- Loop variables become constants after unrolling; data-dependent exit (`while (x != 0)`) with unbounded iterations is not synthesizable.
- Long loops create long combinational paths; to spread work over cycles you must write an FSM/counter instead.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `break` based on data is supported by some tools only when the max bound is static; expect large mux logic.

### Follow-ups
- *How to do 1 bit per clock?* Use a counter register and process `data[cnt]` each cycle.

questions.title: Procedural for loop vs generate-for — when do you use each?
questions.answer: Procedural for describes repeated operations within a process; generate-for replicates instances/declarations at elaboration.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A procedural `for` lives inside an `always`/`initial`/function and describes repeated *operations* (unrolled by synthesis); a generate-`for` lives at module level and replicates *structure* (instances, assigns, declarations) at elaboration.

|  | procedural for | generate for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | inside always/initial/function/task | module scope |
| Loop variable | int / integer | genvar |
| Creates | logic inside one process | instances, nets, always blocks, named scopes |
| Bounds | static for synthesis; dynamic OK in TB | elaboration constants only |
| Typical use | parity, bit-reverse, priority search | N instances of a sub-module, per-lane logic |

```systemverilog
// procedural: one always block, unrolled
always_comb begin
  par = 1'b0;
  for (int i = 0; i < W; i++) par ^= d[i];
end

// generate: N synchronizer instances, each with its own scope
for (genvar g = 0; g < N; g++) begin : g_sync
  sync2 u_sync (.clk(clk), .d(async_in[g]), .q(sync_out[g]));
end
```

### Explanation
- Procedural loops are for algorithmic RTL; generate loops are for structural replication.
- Generate scopes can be referenced hierarchically: `g_sync[3].u_sync.q`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A procedural loop cannot instantiate modules; a generate loop cannot contain blocking procedural statements outside an always block.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a generate loop contain an always block?* Yes, each iteration gets its own always process.

questions.title: Function vs task — what are the differences?
questions.answer: Function returns a value and consumes no time; task can have multiple outputs and timing controls. Functions are better for pure combinational calculations.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A function returns a value (or void), executes in zero time and cannot block; a task can have multiple outputs/inouts and may consume time (`#`, `@`, `wait`). Use functions for pure combinational calculations, tasks for timed TB sequences.

|  | function | task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return value | yes (or void) | no (outputs via arguments) |
| Time-consuming statements | not allowed | allowed |
| Can call | functions only (tasks only via fork..join_none) | functions and tasks |
| Usable in expressions / continuous assign | yes | no |
| Synthesizable | yes (combinational) | yes if no timing controls |

```systemverilog
function automatic logic [7:0] parity8(input logic [63:0] d);
  for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) parity8[i] = ^d[i*8 +: 8];
endfunction

task automatic drive_write(input logic [31:0] addr, data);
  @(posedge vif.clk);
  vif.addr <= addr; vif.wdata <= data; vif.we <= 1'b1;
  @(posedge vif.clk);
  vif.we <= 1'b0;
endtask
```

### Explanation
- Functions keep RTL readable for repeated combinational logic (CRC, ECC, encoders).
- In classes, prefer functions for non-blocking APIs (e.g. `build_phase`) and tasks for anything that waits (`run_phase`, `body`).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Calling a task from a function is a compile error; a function that needs to wait should become a task.

### Follow-ups
- *What is a void function?* A function with no return value; can be called as a statement.

questions.title: Automatic vs static lifetime — what is the difference?
questions.answer: Static vars retain values between calls (re-entrancy issues); automatic vars are per invocation, safe for recursion/concurrency. Class methods are automatic by default.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A static task/function has one copy of its variables shared by all calls (values persist and concurrent calls clobber each other); an automatic one allocates fresh variables per call, so recursion and concurrent calls (e.g. from fork) are safe. Class methods are automatic by default; module tasks/functions are static by default.

```systemverilog
function int cnt_static();   // static by default in a module
  int n;          // single shared copy, initialized once
  n++;
  return n;
endfunction        // returns 1, 2, 3, ...

function automatic int cnt_auto();
  int n = 0;      // new copy each call
  n++;
  return n;
endfunction        // returns 1, 1, 1, ...

function automatic int fact(int n);    // recursion requires automatic
  return (n <= 1) ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1);
endfunction
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T1 as "fork thread 1"
  participant S as "static task vars"
  participant T2 as "fork thread 2"
  T1->>S: addr = 0x10
  T2->>S: addr = 0x20
  S-->>T1: reads 0x20 (clobbered)
```

### Explanation
- Static: storage allocated once at elaboration; good for counters intentionally shared.
- Automatic: storage on a per-call stack; required for recursion and safe concurrency.
- Declare `module automatic` or `program automatic` to change the default for all its tasks.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Automatic variables cannot be referenced hierarchically or used with nonblocking assignment / in `@` from outside.

### Follow-ups
- *Can you mix?* Yes: declare an individual variable `static` inside an automatic function.

questions.title: Are initial blocks synthesizable?
questions.answer: initial is mostly simulation; some FPGAs synthesize init values or memory init. For ASIC, use reset.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** For ASICs, no: `initial` is a simulation construct and silicon flops power up random. Some FPGA flows honor `initial` values and `$readmemh` for register/BRAM initialization because the bitstream configures them, but portable RTL uses reset.

| Target | `initial q = 0;` | `initial $readmemh(...)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ASIC synthesis | ignored (warning) | ignored; use ROM generator |
| FPGA (Xilinx/Intel) | sets power-up value | initializes BRAM/ROM |
| Simulation | sets value at time 0 | loads memory |

```systemverilog
// portable: explicit reset
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) cnt <= '0;
  else        cnt <= cnt + 1'b1;

// FPGA-only ROM init (accepted by most FPGA tools)
logic [7:0] rom [256];
initial $readmemh("rom.hex", rom);
```

### Explanation
- An `initial` assignment in RTL can hide missing-reset bugs: simulation looks fine, silicon starts with X.
- Run some tests with X-initialization (or random init) to catch flops without reset that matter.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Gate-level sims of an ASIC will show X where RTL showed 0 from `initial`.

### Follow-ups
- *Which flops can skip reset?* Datapath flops whose value is always written before being used (saves area).

questions.title: What problems does an incomplete sensitivity list cause?
questions.answer: Incomplete sensitivity lists make simulation miss changes; synthesis builds combinational logic anyway. Use always_comb or @*.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In `always @(a or b)` the block only wakes when a listed signal changes, so if it also reads `c`, simulation holds a stale value while synthesis builds pure combinational logic: a simulation/synthesis mismatch. Use `always_comb` or `@*`.

```systemverilog
// BUG: sel missing from list
always @(a or b)
  y = sel ? a : b;

// FIX
always_comb y = sel ? a : b;
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "a", "wave": "1..........."}, {"name": "b", "wave": "0..........."}, {"name": "sel", "wave": "0..1....0..."}, {"name": "y (sim, buggy)", "wave": "0..........."}, {"name": "y (silicon)", "wave": "0..1....0..."}], "head": {"text": "sim misses the sel change; gate-level/silicon follows it"}}
```

### Explanation
- Synthesis ignores sensitivity lists (with a warning) and builds logic from the code, so RTL sim and netlist sim differ.
- `always_comb` also catches signals read inside called functions, which `@*` misses.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Including extra signals (e.g. the output) is harmless for synthesis but may slow simulation or cause extra evaluation.

### Follow-ups
- *How is it found?* Lint ("incomplete sensitivity list"), or gate-level/equivalence-check mismatch.

questions.title: How do if/else and case infer muxes and priority logic?
questions.answer: if/else and case infer muxes; condition order sets priority when overlapping; make parallel/priority intent explicit.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** An `if/else-if` chain infers priority logic (a cascade of 2:1 muxes, first true condition wins); a `case` with mutually exclusive items infers a parallel mux. The order of overlapping conditions defines priority, and long chains can become timing bottlenecks.

```systemverilog
// priority: req[0] wins
always_comb
  if      (req[0]) gnt = 2'd0;
  else if (req[1]) gnt = 2'd1;
  else if (req[2]) gnt = 2'd2;
  else             gnt = 2'd3;

// parallel mux: sel values never overlap
always_comb
  case (sel)
    2'd0: y = a;  2'd1: y = b;  2'd2: y = c;  default: y = d;
  endcase
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["d"] --> M2["mux req2"]
  C["c"] --> M2
  M2 --> M1["mux req1"]
  B["b"] --> M1
  M1 --> M0["mux req0"]
  A["a"] --> M0
  M0 --> Y["gnt / y"]
```

### Explanation
- Priority chain depth grows with N (N-1 mux levels); a parallel mux is about log2(N) levels.
- Synthesis can flatten priority into parallel logic when conditions are provably exclusive (e.g. one-hot with `unique`).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `if` for exclusive conditions adds unnecessary priority; using `case` with overlapping items silently gives priority to the first item.

### Follow-ups
- *How to make a one-hot mux fast?* AND-OR structure: `y = |({W{sel[0]}} & a) | ...`.

questions.title: What is combinational feedback and why is it dangerous?
questions.answer: Combinational logic feeding itself without storage can oscillate or settle unpredictably; often from RTL coding errors.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A combinational loop is a path from a signal back to itself without a flop. Depending on gate delays it may oscillate, latch unintentionally, or settle unpredictably; STA cannot time it, and simulation can hang in infinite delta cycles.

```systemverilog
// unintended loop: count depends on itself combinationally
always_comb count = count + inc;      // oscillates / hangs simulator

// fix: register the state
always_ff @(posedge clk) count <= count + inc;
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  X["count"] --> ADD["+ inc"] --> X
  X2["count_q (flop)"] --> ADD2["+ inc"] --> D["count_d"] --> X2
```

### Explanation
- Common sources: mux outputs fed back to their own select, cross-coupled always_comb blocks, `assign a = b; assign b = a & c;`.
- Synthesis reports "combinational loop" and STA breaks the loop arbitrarily, so timing results are meaningless.
- Lint tools flag loops; always_comb also warns when its own output is read.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An intentional SR latch built from gates is also a loop; use a library latch cell instead.

### Follow-ups
- *How does simulation behave?* An oscillating loop with zero delay hits the iteration limit (e.g. 'too many delta cycles').

questions.title: What problems do multiple drivers cause?
questions.answer: Multiple drivers produce conflicts, X or tool errors; use a single procedural owner per variable unless deliberate tri-state.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Two drivers on one signal create contention: a resolved net shows X when they disagree, a variable gets last-writer-wins race behavior, and synthesis errors out. Each variable should have exactly one procedural owner, unless a deliberate tri-state/resolved net is intended.

```systemverilog
logic q;
always_ff @(posedge clk) if (set) q <= 1'b1;
always_ff @(posedge clk) if (clr) q <= 1'b0;   // ERROR: q driven by 2 always_ff

// single owner
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  if      (clr) q <= 1'b0;
  else if (set) q <= 1'b1;
```

| Target | Two drivers | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| wire | assign + assign | resolved: X on conflict |
| logic (variable) | two always_ff / always_comb | compile error |
| reg (Verilog) | two always blocks | race; synthesis error |

### Explanation
- `always_ff`/`always_comb` and `logic` make the compiler catch multiple drivers.
- Merging the logic into one block also makes priority explicit (here, clear wins).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Testbench `force` is a separate mechanism and is fine for debug, not for normal stimulus.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you intentionally share a bus?* Use a mux/arbiter internally, tri-states only at I/O pads.

questions.title: How should tri-state logic be written in RTL, and is it used internally?
questions.answer: Internal tri-states become muxes in modern fabrics; use top-level I/O tri-states only; explicit muxing/arbitration internally.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Tri-states (`assign bus = en ? d : 'z;`) are used at top-level I/O pads. Internally, modern ASIC/FPGA fabrics have no tri-state buses; tools convert them into muxes, so write an explicit mux or arbiter instead.

```systemverilog
// top-level bidirectional pad
module io_pad (inout wire pad, input logic oe, dout, output logic din);
  assign pad = oe ? dout : 1'bz;
  assign din = pad;
endmodule

// internal sharing: explicit one-hot mux, not tri-states
always_comb begin
  bus = '0;
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) if (sel[i]) bus |= src[i];
end
```

| en | dout | pad |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | x | z (released) |
| 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |

### Explanation
- An internal tri-state with two enables active at once causes contention and possibly X; with none active it floats.
- Bidirectional ports must be nets (`inout wire`).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- In the testbench, drive an `inout` through a `wire` with an `assign` and its own enable; you cannot drive it procedurally.

### Follow-ups
- *What is a pull-up in SV?* `pullup(pad);` or a `tri1` net gives a weak 1 when not driven.

questions.title: Clock gating vs clock enable — what is the difference?
questions.answer: Clock enable keeps clock running and conditionally updates; clock gating stops the clock for power, needing ICG cells. Don't gate with arbitrary logic.

questions.title: Why is a gated clock built from plain logic risky?
questions.answer: Glitches on derived clocks create unintended edges; ICG cells latch enable during safe phase. Timing/CDC tools must know gated clocks.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** If the enable changes while the clock is high, an AND gate produces a truncated pulse or glitch, which acts as an extra clock edge. An ICG cell latches the enable during the low phase so the enable can only change while the gated clock is held low.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "en (from flop, changes after posedge)", "wave": "0.1..0.."}, {"name": "clk & en (AND)", "wave": "0.hl0hl0"}, {"name": "ICG gclk", "wave": "0..hlhl0"}], "head": {"text": "AND gating: en rising while clk is high creates a short pulse; ICG waits for the next full pulse"}}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  EN["en"] --> L["latch (transparent when clk = 0)"]
  CLK["clk"] --> L
  L --> AND["AND"]
  CLK --> AND
  AND --> GCK["gclk (glitch-free)"]
```

### Explanation
- Latch-based ICG: enable is captured while clk is low, held while clk is high, so the AND output only produces complete pulses.
- STA must see the gated clock as a generated clock and check clock-gating setup/hold on the enable.
- CDC tools must know the gated clock is the same domain as the source clock.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- OR-based gating (for negative-edge flops) needs a flop-on-high-phase latch variant; mismatching them reintroduces glitches.

### Follow-ups
- *Who inserts ICGs?* Synthesis (Power Compiler / Genus) automatically, or RTL instantiation for architectural gating.

questions.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous reset — trade-offs?
questions.answer: Sync reset sampled on clock edge; async reset acts immediately. Assert async, de-assert synchronized to avoid recovery/removal issues.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A synchronous reset is just a data input sampled on the clock edge (needs a running clock); an asynchronous reset forces the flop immediately, independent of the clock. Best practice: assert asynchronously, de-assert synchronously.

```systemverilog
// synchronous
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  if (!rst_n) q <= '0; else q <= d;

// asynchronous
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) q <= '0; else q <= d;
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "rst_n", "wave": "1.0..1.."}, {"name": "q (async)", "wave": "=.0.....", "data": ["5"]}, {"name": "q (sync)", "wave": "=..0....", "data": ["5"]}], "head": {"text": "async reset clears q immediately; sync reset waits for the next edge"}}
```

|  | Sync reset | Async reset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs clock to reset | yes | no |
| Glitch filtering | yes (sampled) | no: glitch resets flop |
| Timing | normal setup/hold on reset path | recovery/removal checks |
| Flop cell | normal flop + mux | flop with CLR/PRE pin |

### Explanation
- Async reset is needed when the clock may be off at power-up or when outputs must be safe immediately.
- Async reset release must meet recovery/removal, hence the reset synchronizer.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A sync reset pulse shorter than a clock period can be missed.

### Follow-ups
- *Which does Xilinx recommend?* Synchronous resets for FPGA fabric efficiency.

questions.title: How do you synchronize reset deassertion? Draw a reset synchronizer.
questions.answer: Asynchronous assertion with synchronous deassertion through a two-flop synchronizer per clock domain.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Use async assert / sync deassert: two flops in the destination domain with their async clear tied to the raw reset and D tied to 1. Reset asserts immediately; release propagates through two flops so every flop in the domain sees the deassertion aligned to a clock edge.

```systemverilog
module rst_sync (input logic clk, input logic arst_n, output logic rst_n_sync);
  logic ff1;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge arst_n)
    if (!arst_n) {rst_n_sync, ff1} <= 2'b00;      // async assert
    else         {rst_n_sync, ff1} <= {ff1, 1'b1}; // sync deassert
endmodule
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p........"}, {"name": "arst_n", "wave": "0..1....."}, {"name": "ff1", "wave": "0...1...."}, {"name": "rst_n_sync", "wave": "0....1..."}], "head": {"text": "assert immediately, release two clocks after arst_n rises"}}
```

### Explanation
- ff1 may go metastable when arst_n rises near a clock edge; ff2 gives it a cycle to resolve.
- One synchronizer per clock domain; the synchronized reset drives the async reset pins of that domain's flops.
- Reset tree of the synchronized reset must still meet recovery/removal in STA.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Do not synchronize reset assertion too; then a domain without a running clock never resets.

### Follow-ups
- *Reset sequencing across domains?* Release resets in an order controlled by a reset controller, often with handshakes.

questions.title: What are recovery and removal timing?
questions.answer: Recovery: release async control before a clock edge; removal: keep asserted around the edge. Violations cause metastability; synchronize deassertion.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** They are setup/hold equivalents for asynchronous control pins (reset/set): **recovery** = minimum time the async reset must be released *before* the clock edge; **removal** = minimum time it must stay asserted *after* the edge. Violations can make the flop go metastable or some flops leave reset one cycle later than others.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "0...1...0...1..."}, {"name": "rst_n (OK: released early)", "wave": "0.1............."}, {"name": "rst_n (recovery viol.)", "wave": "0..1............"}, {"name": "rst_n (removal viol.)", "wave": "0....1.........."}, {"name": "forbidden window", "wave": "0..1.0.........."}], "head": {"text": "rst_n release must fall outside the [edge - recovery, edge + removal] window"}}
```

| Check | Analogy | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recovery | setup | reset deasserted >= t_rec before clk edge |
| Removal | hold | reset stays asserted >= t_rem after clk edge |

### Explanation
- STA reports them as recovery/removal checks on async pins of flops.
- If deassertion is asynchronous to the clock, some flops leave reset at edge N and others at N+1 -> FSMs start in inconsistent states.
- Fix: reset synchronizer so deassertion is aligned to the clock and the reset tree is timed like a data path.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Recovery/removal only matter for *deassertion*; assertion is asynchronous by design.

### Follow-ups
- *What if the reset tree is huge?* Pipeline/duplicate the synchronized reset per region to meet recovery.

questions.title: What are setup and hold time, and how are violations fixed?
questions.answer: Setup: data stable before capturing edge; hold: stable after edge. Violations cause metastability; use STA/CDC since RTL sim doesn't model it.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Setup = data must be stable for t_su before the capturing clock edge; hold = stable for t_h after it. Setup violations depend on clock period (fix: less logic, faster cells, lower frequency); hold violations do not (fix: add delay).

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "0...1..."}, {"name": "data", "wave": "=.=....=", "data": ["old", "new (stable)", ""]}], "head": {"text": "data must not change in the window [edge - t_su, edge + t_h]"}}
```

|  | Setup | Hold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equation | T_clk >= t_cq + t_comb,max + t_su - skew | t_cq + t_comb,min >= t_h + skew |
| Depends on frequency | yes | no |
| Fixes | pipeline, retime, upsize, useful skew, lower freq | insert buffers/delay cells |

### Explanation
- Slack = required - arrival; negative slack is a violation.
- Positive clock skew (capture clock later) helps setup, hurts hold.
- RTL simulation is zero-delay and never shows these; STA and gate-level sim with SDF do.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Hold violations cannot be fixed by slowing the clock: a chip with hold violations fails at every frequency.

### Follow-ups
- *What happens physically on a violation?* The flop can go metastable or capture the wrong value.

questions.title: What is metastability?
questions.answer: Analog condition where a flop can't resolve to valid 0/1 quickly after a marginally-timed transition; two-flop synchronizer reduces but never eliminates it.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** When a flop samples an input changing inside its setup/hold window, its internal node can hang near the mid-rail voltage for an unbounded (exponentially distributed) time before resolving to 0 or 1. Synchronizers give it time to resolve; they reduce the failure probability but never make it zero.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_dst", "wave": "0.1.0.1.0.1."}, {"name": "async_in", "wave": "0..1........"}, {"name": "ff1", "wave": "0.x..1......"}, {"name": "ff2", "wave": "0.....1....."}], "head": {"text": "ff1 may be metastable for part of a cycle; ff2 samples it after it has (very likely) resolved"}}
```

| Quantity | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| MTBF = e^(t_r / tau) / (T_0 x f_clk x f_data) | mean time between failures |
| t_r | resolution time available (about 1 clock period per extra flop) |
| tau, T_0 | process constants of the flop |

### Explanation
- MTBF grows exponentially with resolution time, so each extra synchronizer stage multiplies MTBF enormously.
- Use dedicated synchronizer cells (high-gain, small tau) and place the two flops close together.
- RTL simulation does not model metastability; CDC verification uses structural checks plus metastability injection (random 1-cycle delay).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Metastable output fanning out to several flops can be resolved differently by each -> inconsistent state.

### Follow-ups
- *When to use 3 flops?* Very high frequencies or safety-critical MTBF targets.

questions.title: Explain the two-flop synchronizer.
questions.answer: Two destination-domain flops; first may go metastable, second samples after settling. Not for multi-bit buses.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** For a single-bit level signal crossing into another domain, two back-to-back flops clocked by the destination clock let the first flop's possible metastability resolve for a full cycle before the second flop samples it.

```systemverilog
module sync2 #(parameter int STAGES = 2) (input logic clk_dst, rst_n, d_async, output logic q);
  (* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) logic [STAGES-1:0] sync_ff;   // keep flops together, no retiming
  always_ff @(posedge clk_dst or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) sync_ff <= '0;
    else        sync_ff <= {sync_ff[STAGES-2:0], d_async};
  assign q = sync_ff[STAGES-1];
endmodule
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_src", "wave": "p........."}, {"name": "d (src)", "wave": "0.1......."}, {"name": "clk_dst", "wave": "p........."}, {"name": "ff1", "wave": "0..x1....."}, {"name": "q", "wave": "0....1...."}], "head": {"text": "1-2 cycle latency, possibly varying by one cycle"}}
```

### Explanation
- Only valid for single-bit signals, or multi-bit signals guaranteed to change one bit at a time (Gray code).
- The source signal must be glitch-free (driven directly from a source-domain flop, no combinational logic before the synchronizer).
- The signal must be held long enough for the destination to sample it (at least ~1.5 destination periods).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Latency is non-deterministic (+/- 1 cycle); designs must not depend on the exact cycle.

### Follow-ups
- *Pulses?* Use a toggle synchronizer or handshake.
- *Buses?* Use handshake or async FIFO.

questions.title: Why can't you synchronize a multi-bit bus bit-by-bit?
questions.answer: Independent synchronizers resolve bits on different cycles, creating a mixed word. Use handshake, Gray counter, async FIFO.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Each bit's synchronizer can resolve on a different destination cycle, so for one cycle the destination sees a mix of old and new bits: a value that never existed in the source domain.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_dst", "wave": "p......"}, {"name": "src bus", "wave": "=.=....", "data": ["011", "100"]}, {"name": "bit2 sync", "wave": "0...1.."}, {"name": "bit1 sync", "wave": "1..0..."}, {"name": "bit0 sync", "wave": "1...0.."}, {"name": "dst bus", "wave": "=..==..", "data": ["011", "001 (!)", "100"]}], "head": {"text": "011 -> 100 changes 3 bits; skewed resolution produces a bogus 001"}}
```

| Technique | When to use |
| --- | --- |
| Gray-coded counter + 2FF | pointers/counters that step by 1 |
| req/ack handshake (MCP) | occasional data words |
| async FIFO | streams |
| data held stable + synchronized valid/enable | quasi-static config |

### Explanation
- The valid/enable approach: source holds data stable, toggles a single-bit qualifier; destination samples the bus only after the qualifier is synchronized (multi-cycle path).
- Gray code works only because exactly one bit changes per increment.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Routing skew between bits makes even a 'simultaneous' change arrive at different times.

### Follow-ups
- *Is Gray code enough for any bus?* No, only when the value changes by +/-1 between samples.

questions.title: How do you pass a single-cycle pulse from a fast clock to a slow clock?
questions.answer: Narrow pulses can be missed; convert to level via toggle, handshake, stretcher or async set.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A pulse shorter than the destination period can fall between destination edges and be missed. Convert it to a level (toggle), stretch it, or use a handshake, then edge-detect in the destination domain.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_fast", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "pulse", "wave": "0.10........"}, {"name": "clk_slow", "wave": "h.l.h.l.h.l."}, {"name": "2FF of pulse", "wave": "0..........."}, {"name": "toggle", "wave": "0..1........"}, {"name": "toggle sync", "wave": "0.....1....."}, {"name": "pulse_dst", "wave": "0.......10.."}], "head": {"text": "the raw pulse is never sampled; the toggle level is"}}
```

| Method | Throughput | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pulse stretcher | low | stretch >= 1.5 slow periods |
| toggle synchronizer | 1 event per ~3 dst cycles | simple, no ack |
| req/ack handshake | lower | sender knows when safe |
| async FIFO | high | for bursts of events |

### Explanation
- Fast -> slow is the dangerous direction; slow -> fast with a 2FF and edge detector usually works because the level lasts long enough.
- Toggle: one flop in source flips per event; destination XORs consecutive synchronized samples.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Back-to-back events closer than the sync latency are merged/lost with toggle or stretcher; use a handshake or FIFO.

### Follow-ups
- *How is it verified?* CDC tool checks plus assertion that pulses are spaced far enough apart.

questions.title: Design a toggle (pulse) synchronizer.
questions.answer: Source toggles a bit per event; destination synchronizes and detects change. Needs events separated enough; else handshake/FIFO.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The source flips a toggle flop on each event; the destination synchronizes the level with 2 flops plus a third for edge detection and XORs the last two samples to regenerate a one-cycle pulse.

```systemverilog
module pulse_sync (
  input  logic clk_s, rst_s_n, pulse_s,
  input  logic clk_d, rst_d_n,
  output logic pulse_d);
  logic tog_s;
  logic [2:0] sync_d;
  always_ff @(posedge clk_s or negedge rst_s_n)
    if (!rst_s_n)     tog_s <= 1'b0;
    else if (pulse_s) tog_s <= ~tog_s;          // level change per event
  always_ff @(posedge clk_d or negedge rst_d_n)
    if (!rst_d_n) sync_d <= '0;
    else          sync_d <= {sync_d[1:0], tog_s}; // [0],[1] = 2FF, [2] = history
  assign pulse_d = sync_d[2] ^ sync_d[1];        // one dst-cycle pulse
endmodule
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_s", "wave": "p........."}, {"name": "pulse_s", "wave": "010...10.."}, {"name": "tog_s", "wave": "0.1.....0."}, {"name": "clk_d", "wave": "p........."}, {"name": "sync_d[1]", "wave": "0...1....."}, {"name": "sync_d[2]", "wave": "0....1...."}, {"name": "pulse_d", "wave": "0...10...."}], "head": {"text": "each source pulse becomes one destination pulse"}}
```

### Explanation
- Works in both directions (fast->slow or slow->fast) as long as events are spaced by at least ~2-3 destination cycles.
- No feedback, so the source cannot know whether the event was seen.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Two source pulses within the sync latency produce two toggles that may cancel out -> event lost.

### Follow-ups
- *How to make it safe at high rates?* Add a busy flag fed back by handshake, or use a FIFO.

questions.title: Explain a req/ack handshake for CDC data transfer.
questions.answer: Sender holds data stable with req; waits for synchronized ack before releasing; trades latency for reliability.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The sender puts data on a bus, holds it stable, and raises `req`; the receiver synchronizes `req`, captures data (stable by then), and raises `ack`; the sender synchronizes `ack`, drops `req`, and (4-phase) waits for `ack` to fall. Only single-bit control crosses, the data is sampled when stable.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as "Source domain"
  participant D as "Destination domain"
  S->>S: data <= X (hold stable)
  S->>D: req = 1 (2FF sync)
  D->>D: capture data
  D->>S: ack = 1 (2FF sync)
  S->>D: req = 0
  D->>S: ack = 0
  Note over S,D: 4-phase complete, next word allowed
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_s", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "data", "wave": "x=.........x", "data": ["D0"]}, {"name": "req", "wave": "0.1.....0..."}, {"name": "ack (dst)", "wave": "0....1.....0"}, {"name": "ack_sync (src)", "wave": "0.......1..."}], "head": {"text": "data is stable for the whole req/ack loop"}}
```

### Explanation
- Latency ~ 2 synchronizations each way (4-phase ~ 4 syncs); throughput is low but reliable and clock-ratio independent.
- 2-phase (toggle) handshake halves the latency by treating each transition as an event.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Data must be driven from flops in the source domain and must not change until ack is seen; CDC tools need it declared as a stable/qualified crossing.

### Follow-ups
- *When choose FIFO instead?* When you need one word per cycle throughput.

questions.title: How does an asynchronous FIFO work?
questions.answer: Pointers in separate domains, Gray-coded and synchronized; full/empty computed with synchronized pointers in the respective domains.

questions.title: Why are async FIFO pointers Gray-coded?
questions.answer: Gray code changes one bit between adjacent values, so a synchronized pointer is either old or new, safe to compare.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Consecutive Gray values differ in exactly one bit, so if the synchronizer samples a pointer mid-change, the destination sees either the old or the new value, never a garbage value. With binary, 0111 -> 1000 flips 4 bits and could be sampled as any of 16 values.

| Decimal | Binary | Gray | Bits changed (bin / gray) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 000 | 000 | - |
| 1 | 001 | 001 | 1 / 1 |
| 2 | 010 | 011 | 2 / 1 |
| 3 | 011 | 010 | 1 / 1 |
| 4 | 100 | 110 | 3 / 1 |
| 5 | 101 | 111 | 1 / 1 |
| 6 | 110 | 101 | 2 / 1 |
| 7 | 111 | 100 | 1 / 1 |

```systemverilog
function automatic logic [N-1:0] bin2gray(input logic [N-1:0] b);
  return b ^ (b >> 1);
endfunction
function automatic logic [N-1:0] gray2bin(input logic [N-1:0] g);
  for (int i = N-1; i >= 0; i--) gray2bin[i] = ^(g >> i);
endfunction
```

### Explanation
- An off-by-one sampled pointer only makes full/empty conservative, never wrong.
- The Gray property holds across the wrap (7 -> 0: 100 -> 000) only for power-of-two ranges.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The pointer must advance by at most 1 per source clock, and must come straight from a flop (no glitches).

### Follow-ups
- *Non power of two depth?* Use a different encoding (e.g. Gray range offset) or a handshake-based pointer crossing.

questions.title: How is the async FIFO full condition computed?
questions.answer: Compare next write Gray pointer with synchronized read Gray pointer with upper bits inverted (top two bits for the Cummings scheme).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In the write domain, compare the *next* write Gray pointer with the synchronized read Gray pointer whose two MSBs are inverted: full when the writer is exactly one lap (DEPTH entries) ahead of the reader.

```systemverilog
// AW address bits, pointers are AW+1 bits wide
assign wfull_val = (wgray_next == {~wq2_rgray[AW:AW-1], wq2_rgray[AW-2:0]});
always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n)
  if (!wrst_n) wfull <= 1'b0; else wfull <= wfull_val;
```

| DEPTH = 4 (AW = 2) | binary (3b) | Gray (3b) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rptr = 0 | 000 | 000 |
| wptr = 4 (one lap ahead) | 100 | 110 |
| compare: Gray(w) vs rgray with 2 MSBs inverted |  | 110 == ~(00)0 = 110 -> FULL |

### Explanation
- In binary, full is `wbin[AW] != rbin[AW] && wbin[AW-1:0] == rbin[AW-1:0]`.
- In Gray, the second MSB also flips between laps, hence the inversion of the top **two** bits.
- Using the *next* pointer makes `full` registered and asserted the same cycle the last slot is written.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Inverting only the MSB in Gray form is a classic bug: it never matches correctly.

### Follow-ups
- *Almost-full?* Convert synced rgray to binary and subtract.

questions.title: How is the async FIFO empty condition computed?
questions.answer: Empty when the next read Gray pointer equals the synchronized write Gray pointer, compared in the read domain; reset alignment essential.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In the read domain, empty is asserted when the next read Gray pointer equals the write Gray pointer synchronized into the read domain. Reset must initialize both pointers to the same value so the FIFO starts empty.

```systemverilog
assign rempty_val = (rgray_next == rq2_wgray);
always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n)
  if (!rrst_n) rempty <= 1'b1;            // empty out of reset
  else         rempty <= rempty_val;
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "wclk", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "winc", "wave": "0.10........"}, {"name": "rclk", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rq2_wgray", "wave": "=.....=.....", "data": ["000", "001"]}, {"name": "rempty", "wave": "1......0..10"}, {"name": "rinc", "wave": "0.........10"}], "head": {"text": "empty deasserts ~2-3 rclk after the write (sync latency), reasserts right after the read"}}
```

### Explanation
- Equality of all bits (including the wrap bit) means same lap, same address -> empty.
- Because the write pointer is seen late, `empty` stays asserted a few cycles longer than necessary: safe pessimism.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Asserting reset in one domain only can leave pointers mismatched -> phantom data; reset both domains together.

### Follow-ups
- *Almost-empty?* Requires gray-to-binary conversion of the synced pointer.

questions.title: Can you build an async FIFO with a non-power-of-two depth?
questions.answer: Classic Gray-pointer FIFOs need power-of-two depth; non-power-of-two requires extra logic or different architecture.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Not with the classic Gray-pointer design: wrapping a binary counter at a non-power-of-two value (e.g. 5 -> 0) changes several Gray bits at once, breaking the one-bit-change property. You need extra logic or another architecture.

| Depth 6, naive wrap | binary | Gray | bits changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 -> 5 | 100 -> 101 | 110 -> 111 | 1 |
| 5 -> 0 (wrap) | 101 -> 000 | 111 -> 000 | **3 (unsafe)** |

| Option | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Round depth up to power of two | simplest; e.g. 6 -> 8 |
| Symmetric Gray range | count over the middle 2N codes of a 2^k Gray sequence so wrap changes one bit (even depths only) |
| Handshake-synchronized binary pointers | transfer pointer value with req/ack (lower update rate) |
| Credit-based flow control | count credits instead of comparing pointers |

### Explanation
- `$clog2(DEPTH)` only sizes the pointers; it does not make wrap-around CDC-safe.
- Even depths can use a Gray sub-sequence trick; odd depths cannot keep the single-bit property across wrap.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Sync FIFOs (single clock) can be any depth: binary pointers with explicit wrap and a counter are fine.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not just use a 2^n FIFO?* Usually that is the answer unless area is critical.

questions.title: Are blocking assignments allowed inside a clocked always block?
questions.answer: Legal but model immediate sequential updates rather than parallel register updates; use NBAs for state, blocking only for careful temporaries.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** They are legal but model immediate sequential updates: a variable assigned with `=` and read later in the same block becomes combinational logic, while one read before its assignment or outside the block becomes a flop. NBAs are clearer and avoid inter-block races; blocking is only acceptable for block-local temporaries.

```systemverilog
always @(posedge clk) begin
  b = a;      // b: flop (read by other blocks -> RACE)
  c = b;      // c: flop fed by a (b's new value) -> one stage, not two
end

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  b <= a;     // two-stage pipeline, order-independent
  c <= b;
end
```

| Style | b | c | Pipeline depth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| blocking | flop of a | flop of a (same as b) | 1 |
| nonblocking | flop of a | flop of b | 2 |

### Explanation
- If another always block reads `b` at the same edge, it may get the old or new value -> race.
- Mixing blocking for temporaries and NBA for state inside one `always_ff` is accepted by many teams if temporaries are declared locally.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Lint rule: no blocking assignment to a variable that is read outside its block.

### Follow-ups
- *Can the same variable use both?* No: illegal in always_ff and a lint error elsewhere.

questions.title: How do you use temporary variables in sequential logic without creating extra registers?
questions.answer: Temp assigned and consumed in the same clocked process creates no register; NBAs determine the state elements.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Declare the temporary inside the clocked block, assign it with `=` *before* reading it, and read it only in that block in the same clock; it then synthesizes as combinational logic, and only the NBA targets become flops.

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  logic [8:0] sum;          // automatic temp, local to this block
  sum = a + b;              // combinational
  if (sum[8]) acc <= 8'hFF; // saturate
  else        acc <= sum[7:0];
end
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["a"] --> ADD["+ (sum, combinational)"]
  B["b"] --> ADD
  ADD --> SAT["saturate mux"] --> ACC["acc (flop)"]
```

### Explanation
- A temp that is read *before* it is written in the block would need its previous-cycle value -> a flop is inferred.
- Declaring it inside the `begin...end` prevents other blocks from reading it.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Some lint/coding standards still forbid `=` in always_ff; then compute the temp in an `always_comb` instead.

### Follow-ups
- *Is the temp visible in waves?* Often not after synthesis; in RTL sim yes.

questions.title: What is the recommended combinational next-state FSM coding style?
questions.answer: Separate next-state logic from state registers; default next_state = state to avoid latches.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Separate the state register (`always_ff`) from next-state/output logic (`always_comb`); in the combinational block default `next_state = state` and default all outputs, then override in the case items. This avoids latches and makes the registered state explicit.

```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, REQ, WAIT_ACK} state_e;
state_e state, next_state;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) state <= IDLE;
  else        state <= next_state;

always_comb begin
  next_state = state;   // default: stay
  req_o      = 1'b0;    // default outputs
  unique case (state)
    IDLE:     if (start) next_state = REQ;
    REQ:      begin req_o = 1'b1; next_state = WAIT_ACK; end
    WAIT_ACK: begin req_o = 1'b1; if (ack) next_state = IDLE; end
    default:  next_state = IDLE;
  endcase
end
```

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> IDLE
  IDLE --> REQ: start
  REQ --> WAIT_ACK
  WAIT_ACK --> IDLE: ack
  WAIT_ACK --> WAIT_ACK: !ack
```

### Explanation
- Two-process style keeps timing clear: everything in always_comb is combinational.
- Registered outputs (three-process) can be added when outputs must be glitch-free.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forgetting the `next_state = state` default creates latches.

### Follow-ups
- *One-process FSM?* Fine but outputs become registered one cycle later.

questions.title: Moore vs Mealy FSM — what is the difference?
questions.answer: Moore outputs depend only on state; Mealy on state and inputs, faster but may glitch.
questions.solution:
