**Key idea:** Moore outputs depend only on the current state (change only after a clock edge, glitch-free if registered); Mealy outputs depend on state and inputs (react in the same cycle, usually fewer states, but can glitch and create long combinational paths).

|  | Moore | Mealy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Output depends on | state | state + inputs |
| Latency | 1 cycle after input | same cycle |
| States for '101' detector | 4 | 3 |
| Glitch risk | low | inputs propagate to outputs |

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  S0 --> S1: 1/0
  S1 --> S2: 0/0
  S2 --> S1: 1/1
  S1 --> S1: 1/0
  S0 --> S0: 0/0
  S2 --> S0: 0/0
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p......"}, {"name": "in", "wave": "1.01..."}, {"name": "mealy_out", "wave": "0..10.."}, {"name": "moore_out", "wave": "0...10."}], "head": {"text": "Mealy asserts during the cycle the last '1' arrives; Moore one cycle later"}}
```

### Explanation
- The diagram is a Mealy overlapping '101' detector (output on transition).
- A Moore version needs an extra S3 state whose output is 1.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Mealy outputs feeding another Mealy FSM can form combinational loops.

### Follow-ups
- *How to make a Mealy output glitch-free?* Register it (then it behaves with Moore timing).

questions.title: One-hot vs binary FSM encoding — trade-offs?
questions.answer: Binary uses ~log2(N) flops; one-hot uses N flops but simpler decode and often faster; choice depends on area/timing/power.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Binary uses ceil(log2 N) flops but needs decode logic; one-hot uses N flops, each state decode is a single bit, giving faster next-state logic (popular on FPGAs with abundant flops). Gray encoding minimizes toggles for sequential state sequences.

| Encoding | Flops (N=8) | State decode | Speed | Power |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| binary | 3 | 3-input compare | slower | few flops, more toggles |
| one-hot | 8 | 1 bit | fast | 2 flops toggle per transition |
| Gray | 3 | 3-input compare | medium | 1 toggle for sequential transitions |

```systemverilog
// one-hot with enum: explicit values
typedef enum logic [3:0] {IDLE = 4'b0001, RD = 4'b0010, WR = 4'b0100, DONE = 4'b1000} st_e;
// reverse-case idiom for one-hot decode
always_comb begin
  next = st_e'('0);
  unique case (1'b1)
    state[0]: next = start ? RD : IDLE;
    state[1]: next = WR;
    state[2]: next = DONE;
    state[3]: next = IDLE;
  endcase
end
```

### Explanation
- Synthesis can re-encode FSMs automatically (FSM extraction) unless told to preserve encoding.
- ASIC choice depends on state count, timing, area, power and safety requirements.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- One-hot has many illegal states (2^N - N); add recovery logic or assertions.

### Follow-ups
- *Safe FSM?* Tools can add Hamming-distance-3 encodings and recovery for radiation environments.

questions.title: How do you handle illegal states in an FSM?
questions.answer: Include default transition to a known state and assertions that the state is legal; one-hot can be zero-hot/multi-hot.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Add a `default` transition to a known safe state, assert that the state is always legal (e.g. `$onehot(state)`), and if required by safety specs, ask synthesis to keep the recovery logic ("safe FSM"), because it may otherwise optimize the unreachable default away.

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  next_state = state;
  case (state)
    IDLE: ...;
    RUN : ...;
    default: next_state = IDLE;          // recover from illegal codes
  endcase
end

// one-hot sanity
a_onehot: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $onehot(state))
  else $error("illegal FSM state %b", state);
```

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  IDLE --> RUN: start
  RUN --> IDLE: done
  ILLEGAL --> IDLE: default branch
  RUN --> ILLEGAL: SEU / X / bug
```

### Explanation
- Illegal states come from bugs, X propagation, uninitialized flops, or single-event upsets.
- Zero-hot and multi-hot are the illegal patterns for one-hot encoding.
- Synthesis treats unreachable states as don't care; use the tool's safe-FSM attribute to keep recovery.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `unique case` without default plus an illegal state yields a runtime warning but undefined hardware behavior.

### Follow-ups
- *How to verify recovery?* Force the state register to an illegal value in simulation or use formal.

questions.title: What are the advantages of SystemVerilog enums?
questions.answer: Enums name states/modes with packed representation, improve readability, type checking and waveform debug.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Enums give names to encodings (readable code and waveforms), are strongly typed (assigning a plain int needs a cast), can have explicit base types/values, and provide methods like `.name()`, `.next()`, `.first()`, `.num()`.

```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE = 2'b00, RUN = 2'b01, DONE = 2'b10} state_e;
state_e st;
st = RUN;                 // ok
// st = 2'b01;            // error: int -> enum needs a cast
st = state_e'(2'b01);     // explicit cast
$display("state = %s", st.name());   // prints RUN
for (state_e s = s.first(); ; s = s.next()) begin
  $display("%s", s.name());
  if (s == s.last()) break;
end
```

| Method | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| first()/last() | first/last member |
| next(N)/prev(N) | member N away (wraps) |
| num() | number of members |
| name() | string name |

### Explanation
- Waveform viewers show names instead of raw bits.
- Out-of-range values (via cast) are possible; `$cast` checks legality.
- Enums are packed, so they synthesize to the base type.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- 4-state base type defaults to X at sim start; 2-state (`int`) enums default to the first member's value only if it is 0.

### Follow-ups
- *Enum in randomization?* `rand state_e s;` randomizes only among legal members.

questions.title: Packed vs unpacked arrays — what is the difference?
questions.answer: Packed dimensions are part of the vector (bitwise ops); unpacked are separate elements (memories, collections).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Packed dimensions (left of the name) form one contiguous bit vector usable in arithmetic/bitwise ops and slicing; unpacked dimensions (right of the name) are separate elements, like an array of words or a memory.

```systemverilog
logic [3:0][7:0] pk;     // packed: 32-bit vector, pk[2] is a byte
logic [7:0] up [4];      // unpacked: 4 separate bytes
logic [7:0] mem [0:1023];// memory: maps to RAM

pk = 32'hDEAD_BEEF;      // whole-vector assignment
pk[0] = 8'hEF;           // byte select
up = '{8'h1, 8'h2, 8'h3, 8'h4};   // assignment pattern
// up = 32'h0;           // ERROR: cannot assign a vector to unpacked array
{>>{up}} = pk;           // streaming operator to convert
```

|  | Packed | Unpacked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declared | `logic [3:0][7:0] a` | `logic [7:0] a [4]` |
| Treated as integer | yes | no |
| Element types | bit-level types only | any type (class, real, struct) |
| Typical use | buses, structured fields | memories, collections |

### Explanation
- Packed structs/unions also form vectors.
- Indexing order: unpacked dims first, then packed: `logic [3:0][7:0] x [2]` -> `x[1][3][7]`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Large packed arrays are slow in simulation; memories should be unpacked.

### Follow-ups
- *Dynamic/associative/queue arrays?* All unpacked kinds used in testbenches.

questions.title: How do synthesis tools infer memories, and what is read-during-write behavior?
questions.answer: Coding style (sync read/write), depth, width and target decide RAM vs flops; read-during-write must be explicit.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Coding a memory array with a synchronous write and a (preferably) registered read lets tools map it to block RAM/SRAM; asynchronous reads map to LUTRAM or flops. When reading and writing the same address in one cycle you must define whether the read returns old data (read-first), new data (write-first) or is undefined.

```systemverilog
module sp_ram #(parameter int DW = 32, AW = 10) (input logic clk, we,
       input logic [AW-1:0] addr, input logic [DW-1:0] wdata, output logic [DW-1:0] rdata);
  logic [DW-1:0] mem [2**AW];
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (we) mem[addr] <= wdata;
    rdata <= mem[addr];        // read-first (old data) because of NBA
  end
endmodule
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p....."}, {"name": "we", "wave": "0.10.."}, {"name": "addr", "wave": "=.=...", "data": ["A", "A"]}, {"name": "wdata", "wave": "x.=x..", "data": ["NEW"]}, {"name": "rdata (read-first)", "wave": "x.=.=.", "data": ["OLD", "NEW"]}, {"name": "rdata (write-first)", "wave": "x.=...", "data": ["NEW"]}], "head": {"text": "same-address read during write"}}
```

### Explanation
- Read-first vs write-first is determined by coding: `rdata <= we ? wdata : mem[addr]` gives write-first.
- ASIC SRAMs are instantiated from memory compilers; behavioral models must match their read-during-write spec.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An asynchronous reset on the memory array or a read with reset prevents BRAM inference.

### Follow-ups
- *Dual-port with two clocks?* Read-during-write across ports is often undefined; avoid or arbitrate.

questions.title: What read-during-write modes exist for memories, and how do you code each?
questions.answer: Same-address read/write may return old, new, or device-specific data; consult macro/FPGA docs and code to the required mode.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** For a same-address read and write in the same cycle, a memory can return old data (read-first), new data (write-first / write-through), or keep the previous output (no-change); some dual-port macros leave it undefined. Code the mode the target macro actually implements, and check its datasheet.

| Mode | rdata when we && raddr == waddr | RTL pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| read-first | old mem[addr] | `rdata <= mem[addr];` (NBA, write in same block) |
| write-first | wdata | `rdata <= we ? wdata : mem[addr];` |
| no-change | previous rdata | `if (!we) rdata <= mem[addr];` |
| undefined (true dual-port, 2 clocks) | X / garbage | avoid by arbitration or add assertion |

```systemverilog
// write-first single-port
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (we) mem[addr] <= wdata;
  rdata <= we ? wdata : mem[addr];
end

// flag the undefined case in a dual-port model
a_no_collision: assert property (@(posedge clk) !(we_a && re_b && addr_a == addr_b));
```

### Explanation
- Simulation of a behavioral model shows whatever the RTL was coded to do; the silicon macro may behave differently, so the model must match the macro spec.
- Bypass logic (forwarding wdata) can implement write-first on top of a read-first macro.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Collision on a true dual-port SRAM with two clocks can corrupt the *written* data too on some macros.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you verify it?* Directed same-address tests plus a cover property on the collision condition.

questions.title: What causes synthesis vs simulation mismatches?
questions.answer: RTL semantics differ from hardware: incomplete sensitivity, #delays, init assumptions, X-optimism, ambiguous reset. Lint, CDC, formal, GLS expose them.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Mismatches arise when simulation semantics of RTL differ from how synthesis interprets it: incomplete sensitivity lists, `#` delays, `initial` values, X-optimism, `full_case/parallel_case` pragmas, casex, and ambiguous resets. Catch them with lint, gate-level simulation, formal equivalence and X-prop.

| Cause | RTL sim | Synthesized hardware |
| --- | --- | --- |
| incomplete sensitivity list | misses changes | pure combinational |
| `#5` delays | delayed | ignored |
| `initial q = 0` | q starts 0 | random power-up (ASIC) |
| `// synopsys full_case` | latch/hold for missing items | don't care -> optimized |
| X on `if` condition | takes else branch | either branch |
| casex with X selector | matches an item | unknown |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  RTL["RTL"] --> LINT["Lint"]
  RTL --> SIM["RTL simulation"]
  RTL --> SYN["Synthesis"] --> NET["Netlist"]
  NET --> LEC["Formal equivalence vs RTL"]
  NET --> GLS["Gate-level sim"]
```

### Explanation
- Formal equivalence (LEC) proves netlist == RTL, but it uses the same interpretation as synthesis (pragmas, X as don't care), so it cannot catch every simulation-only mismatch; GLS catches X/reset/initialization issues.
- Coding guidelines: `always_comb`, no delays in RTL, explicit resets, `unique/priority` instead of pragmas.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Mismatches can pass all RTL tests and only appear in silicon or GLS.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is GLS still used?* Reset/X issues, timing annotation (SDF), power-up behavior, DFT logic.

questions.title: What is X-optimism in RTL simulation?
questions.answer: if/case give a definite result when the control is X, hiding unknown states; use assertions, case equality, unique case, X-prop.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** RTL `if`/`case` statements treat an X condition as false (or match no item) and pick a definite branch, so the X disappears even though real hardware could take either path. This hides bugs like missing resets.

```systemverilog
logic sel = 1'bx;      // e.g. un-reset flop
always_comb
  if (sel) y = a;      // X is not true -> else branch
  else     y = b;      // RTL: y = b (looks fine!)
// hardware: y could be a or b -> real bug hidden
```

| Construct | sel = X behavior | Hardware reality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| if (sel) | else branch | a or b |
| case (sel) | default / no match | any item |
| y = sel ? a : b | bitwise merge: X where a != b | a or b (this one is accurate) |

### Explanation
- Mitigations: `assert (!$isunknown(sel))` on control signals, `unique case` (warns on no-match), X-prop simulation modes (e.g. VCS `-xprop`, Xcelium X-prop) that make if/case propagate X.
- Reset all control flops; datapath flops can stay un-reset if validated by control.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Tests that pass in RTL may fail in GLS because GLS doesn't have the optimism.

### Follow-ups
- *What does the ternary do with X?* Merges a and b bitwise: bits where they agree stay known.

questions.title: What is X-pessimism in gate-level simulation?
questions.answer: GLS produces X where hardware resolves deterministically, e.g. mux with X select and equal inputs; X-prop balances optimism/pessimism.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Gate-level models can produce X where real hardware is deterministic: e.g. a mux with select = X and both data inputs equal to 1 still gives 1 in silicon, but some cell models output X. It causes false failures that waste debug time.

| Logic | Inputs | Hardware | Pessimistic GLS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mux | a=1, b=1, sel=X | 1 | X (in some cell models) |
| y = (s & a) | (~s & a) | a=1, s=X | 1 | X |
| reconvergent X | x ^ x | 0 | X |

```systemverilog
// RTL ternary is accurate here: equal inputs give a known output
assign y = sel ? a : b;      // sel=X, a=b=1 -> y=1
// gate-level AND-OR implementation: (sel & a) | (~sel & b)
// sel=X -> (X & 1) | (X & 1) = X | X = X  -> pessimistic
```

### Explanation
- Optimism (RTL) hides bugs; pessimism (GLS) reports false bugs. X-prop modes try to balance by computing the merge of all possible branch results.
- Fix GLS pessimism by resetting the offending flops or using initialization only for verified-don't-care flops (not by blindly forcing).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Blanket `+initreg` random initialization can also hide real reset bugs.

### Follow-ups
- *Formal X analysis?* Some formal tools prove whether an X can reach outputs (X-propagation checks).

questions.title: force/release vs procedural assignment — when do you use force?
questions.answer: force overrides drivers until release; debug/testbench feature only. Deposit sets without overriding drivers.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `force` overrides all other drivers of a net/variable until `release`; it is a debug/testbench tool (error injection, bypassing blocks), never synthesizable RTL. A procedural assignment is just one driver update and can be overwritten by the next one; 'deposit' (simulator API, e.g. `$deposit`/UVM `uvm_hdl_deposit`) sets a value once without holding it.

```systemverilog
initial begin
  #100 force dut.u_core.pll_lock = 1'b1;   // hold regardless of drivers
  #500 release dut.u_core.pll_lock;        // design drives again

  // UVM backdoor equivalents
  void'(uvm_hdl_force  ("tb.dut.err_inj", 1'b1));
  void'(uvm_hdl_deposit("tb.dut.cnt",     8'hFE)); // design may overwrite next cycle
  void'(uvm_hdl_release("tb.dut.err_inj"));
end
```

| Operation | Overrides drivers | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| procedural `=`/`<=` | no (variable updated once) | until next write |
| force | yes | until release |
| deposit | no | until design drives again |

### Explanation
- After `release` on a variable, it keeps the forced value until the next procedural write; a net immediately takes its driver's value.
- Forcing internal signals couples the TB to hierarchy; keep forces in a dedicated error-injection component.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forcing a signal in a gate-level netlist may fail because names change after synthesis.

### Follow-ups
- *Use in UVM?* Typically via `uvm_hdl_force` in an error-injection sequence.

questions.title: $display vs $strobe vs $monitor?
questions.answer: $display prints immediately; $strobe prints at end of time step after NBA; $monitor prints when arguments change.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `$display` prints immediately when executed (Active region, may show pre-NBA values); `$strobe` prints once at the end of the time step (Postponed, settled values); `$monitor` prints whenever any argument changes (Postponed).

```systemverilog
always @(posedge clk) begin
  q <= d;
  $display("display q=%0d", q);   // OLD q
  $strobe ("strobe  q=%0d", q);   // NEW q (after NBA)
end
initial $monitor("%0t a=%0b b=%0b", $time, a, b);  // prints on every change of a or b
```

| Task | When | Values | How often |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $display | immediately | current (may be pre-NBA) | each call |
| $write | immediately, no newline | current | each call |
| $strobe | end of time step | final | once per call |
| $monitor | end of time step | final | whenever an arg changes |

### Explanation
- Only one `$monitor` is active at a time; `$monitoroff/$monitoron` control it.
- In UVM, prefer `uvm_info` (verbosity, IDs, report catcher) over raw `$display`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `$strobe` called from multiple processes still prints in unspecified order.

### Follow-ups
- *Fully settled sample in SVA?* Assertions use Preponed sampled values instead.

questions.title: What do $timeformat, timeunit and timeprecision do?
questions.answer: timeunit/timeprecision define a module's time scale/precision; prefer explicit declarations over inherited `timescale.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `timeunit` sets the unit for delay numbers in a scope (e.g. `#5` = 5 ns), `timeprecision` sets the rounding resolution; `$timeformat(units, precision, suffix, width)` controls how `%t` prints times.

```systemverilog
module tb;
  timeunit 1ns;
  timeprecision 1ps;
  initial begin
    $timeformat(-9, 3, " ns", 10);    // print %t in ns with 3 decimals
    #2.5;                             // 2.500 ns
    $display("now = %t", $realtime); // "now =   2.500 ns"
  end
endmodule
```

| $timeformat arg | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| units | power of 10 (-9 = ns, -12 = ps) | -9 |
| precision | digits after the decimal point | 3 |
| suffix | string appended | " ns" |
| min width | field width | 10 |

### Explanation
- Delays are rounded to the precision: with 1 ns / 1 ps, `#1.2345` becomes about 1.235 ns (1235 ps).
- The simulator's global precision is the finest precision of all modules.
- `$time` returns an integer in the module's unit (rounded); `$realtime` returns a real.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `$time` in a 1ns-unit module when events happen at 0.5 ns shows rounded values.

### Follow-ups
- *How is `#1step` defined?* One global precision unit; used in clocking block input skew.

questions.title: `timescale vs timeunit/timeprecision — which is better?
questions.answer: `timescale is a preprocessor directive affecting subsequent files; timeunit/timeprecision are scoped language constructs, clearer and order-independent.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `` `timescale`` is a compiler directive that applies to every following file until another `` `timescale``, so its effect depends on file compilation order; `timeunit`/`timeprecision` are language declarations scoped to the module/package/program/interface they are in, so they are order-independent.

```systemverilog
`timescale 1ns/1ps      // file a.sv: also applies to b.sv if compiled after a.sv
module a; endmodule

module b;               // b.sv: explicit, unaffected by compile order
  timeunit 1ns;
  timeprecision 1ps;
endmodule

// SV-2009 shorthand
module c; timeunit 1ns / 1ps; endmodule
```

|  | `timescale | timeunit / timeprecision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kind | preprocessor directive | language construct |
| Scope | all subsequent compilation | enclosing design element |
| Compile-order sensitive | yes | no |
| Missing | tool default or error if some files have it | inherits from `timescale or default |

### Explanation
- Many simulators error when some modules have a timescale and others don't.
- Precedence: a `timeunit` declaration in a module overrides any `` `timescale`` for that module.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A package compiled first with no time declarations may pick up the tool default (often 1s!).

### Follow-ups
- *Command-line override?* e.g. `-timescale=1ns/1ps` for files with none.

questions.title: Can # delay controls be used in synthesizable RTL?
questions.answer: # delays model simulation timing and don't synthesize; RTL describes logic, timing constraints decide physical delay.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Synthesis ignores `#` delays (with a warning) because physical delay comes from cells and wires, constrained by SDC and verified by STA. In RTL they only change simulation, which risks sim/synth mismatch, so keep them out of RTL (except sometimes a small `#1` on flop outputs in legacy code for waveform readability).

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) q <= #1 d;   // simulation-only, synthesis ignores
assign #2 y = a & b;                   // ignored by synthesis
// timing intent belongs in SDC:
//   create_clock -period 2.0 [get_ports clk]
//   set_max_delay 1.5 -from [get_ports a] -to [get_ports y]
```

| Where | # delay OK? |
| --- | --- |
| Synthesizable RTL | no (ignored) |
| Testbench stimulus | yes |
| Behavioral models (memories, PLL) | yes |
| Gate-level | from SDF / specify blocks |

### Explanation
- Zero-delay RTL plus STA is the standard flow; timing is never verified by RTL simulation.
- `#1` on NBAs can mask race conditions in the testbench rather than fixing them.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Delays inside an `always_comb` are illegal.

### Follow-ups
- *How to model a clock in a TB?* `always #5 clk = ~clk;` with an explicit timeunit.

questions.title: Transport vs inertial delay — what is the difference?
questions.answer: Inertial delay suppresses pulses shorter than the delay; transport preserves them. RTL synthesis doesn't use # delays.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Inertial delay (default for continuous assigns and gates) filters pulses shorter than the delay, like a real gate's capacitance; transport delay (modeled with a delayed NBA, `q <= #d x`) passes every pulse, like an ideal wire.

```systemverilog
assign #3 y_inertial = a;                  // pulses < 3 are swallowed
always @(a) y_transport <= #3 a;            // every edge reproduced 3 units later
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "a", "wave": "0.10..1...0."}, {"name": "y_inertial (#3)", "wave": "0.....1...0."}, {"name": "y_transport (#3)", "wave": "0...10..1..."}], "head": {"text": "the 1-unit-wide pulse on a is filtered by inertial delay but kept by transport delay (not to exact scale)"}}
```

### Explanation
- SDF back-annotation uses pulse-rejection limits (PATHPULSE) to control which pulses become X or are filtered.
- Synthesis ignores both; they are only modeling concepts.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Blocking `#3 y = a;` inside an always block delays the whole process and misses events that happen during the wait.

### Follow-ups
- *Use in TB?* Transport-style delays model board/cable delays in interface BFMs.

questions.title: What are specify blocks used for?
questions.answer: Specify blocks describe path delays and timing checks for gate-level simulation; not synthesizable RTL.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A `specify ... endspecify` block in a (usually cell-level) module describes pin-to-pin path delays and timing checks (`$setup`, `$hold`, `$width`...). SDF back-annotation fills in the actual delays for gate-level simulation. They are not synthesizable functional RTL.

```systemverilog
module DFF (input D, CK, output reg Q);
  always @(posedge CK) Q <= D;
  specify
    specparam tCQ = 0.12, tSU = 0.05, tH = 0.02;
    (posedge CK => (Q +: D)) = tCQ;        // clock-to-Q path delay
    $setup(D, posedge CK, tSU);
    $hold (posedge CK, D, tH);
  endspecify
endmodule
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  LIB["cell library .v (specify blocks)"] --> GLS["gate-level simulation"]
  SDF["SDF from STA / P&R"] -->|annotate delays| GLS
  NET["netlist"] --> GLS
```

### Explanation
- Parallel `=>` and full `*>` path connections; edge-sensitive and state-dependent paths are allowed.
- Timing-check violations print messages and can make the output X via notifier registers.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Running GLS without SDF uses the specparam defaults or unit delays; results do not reflect real timing.

### Follow-ups
- *Who writes them?* Library vendors; designers rarely do.

questions.title: How do $setup/$hold timing checks in simulation relate to STA?
questions.answer: $setup/$hold report violations in gate-level/timing models; they don't replace STA.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** System timing checks (`$setup`, `$hold`, `$setuphold`, `$recovery`, `$width`, `$period`) in cell models report violations during gate-level simulation for the vectors actually simulated; STA checks all paths exhaustively without vectors. Simulation checks complement, never replace, STA.

```systemverilog
specify
  $setuphold(posedge CK, D, 0.05, 0.02, notifier);   // violation -> notifier toggles
  $recovery (posedge RN, posedge CK, 0.10);
  $width    (posedge CK, 0.30);
endspecify
// UDP flop sets Q = X when notifier toggles
```

|  | Timing checks in GLS | STA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coverage | only simulated scenarios | all paths |
| Needs vectors | yes | no |
| Finds | async crossings, real violations in tests, X from notifier | setup/hold/recovery on all paths |
| Speed | slow | fast |

### Explanation
- CDC synchronizer first-stage flops legitimately violate setup/hold; disable checks on those (e.g. `$setuphold` with `+notimingcheck` per instance) or they produce X.
- GLS with SDF is used to validate constraints (false/multicycle paths) and reset/initialization behavior.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Turning off all timing checks globally hides real problems.

### Follow-ups
- *What is a notifier?* A reg toggled on violation that the UDP uses to force X.

questions.title: Immediate vs concurrent assertions?
questions.answer: Immediate assertions execute when procedural control reaches them; concurrent assertions sample on clock events and describe temporal relations.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Immediate assertions are procedural statements checked when execution reaches them (like an `if`); concurrent assertions are clocked, sample values in the Preponed region, and describe temporal behavior across cycles.

```systemverilog
// immediate: in procedural code
always_comb begin
  a_onehot: assert ($onehot0(gnt)) else $error("multiple grants %b", gnt);
end

// concurrent: temporal, clocked
a_req_ack: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                            req |-> ##[1:3] ack)
           else $error("ack not within 3 cycles");
```

|  | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location | procedural code | module/interface/program/checker or procedural (inferred clock) |
| Timing | evaluated when executed | every clock tick |
| Multi-cycle behavior | no | yes (sequences) |
| Sampling | current values (deferred variants exist) | Preponed sampled values |
| Formal tools | limited | first-class |

### Explanation
- Deferred immediate assertions (`assert #0` / `assert final`) avoid glitch failures in combinational code.
- Concurrent assertions are the main tool for protocol, FSM, and handshake checks and are bindable with `bind`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An immediate assertion in an `always_comb` can fire on zero-time glitches; use `assert final`.

### Follow-ups
- *Where do action blocks run?* Reactive region for concurrent assertions.

questions.title: SVA |-> vs |=> implication?
questions.answer: |-> overlapped: consequent starts same cycle; |=> non-overlapped: one clock later.

questions.title: What do $past, $rose and $fell do in SVA?
questions.answer: $past gets a previous sampled value; $rose/$fell detect 0->1 and 1->0 transitions.

questions.title: What does disable iff do in an assertion?
questions.answer: disable iff turns off a concurrent assertion while reset or another condition is true, avoiding false failures.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `disable iff (expr)` asynchronously aborts any in-progress attempt and suppresses new ones while `expr` is true, so resets do not produce false failures. Aborted attempts count as disabled, not passed/failed.

```systemverilog
a_req_ack: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req |-> ##[1:4] ack);

// default for all assertions in the scope
default disable iff (!rst_n);
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p........."}, {"name": "rst_n", "wave": "1...0..1.."}, {"name": "req", "wave": "0.1......."}, {"name": "ack", "wave": "0........."}, {"name": "attempt", "wave": "0.=.x.....", "data": ["running", ""]}], "head": {"text": "reset asserted mid-attempt: the attempt is disabled, no failure reported"}}
```

### Explanation
- The disable condition is evaluated asynchronously (current values, not sampled), unlike the property itself.
- Only one `disable iff` per property; nested not allowed.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `disable iff` with a signal that glitches can randomly cancel checks; use a clean synchronized reset.

### Follow-ups
- *Cover with disable iff?* Disabled attempts are not counted as covered.

questions.title: What is a cover property and why use it?
questions.answer: cover property checks that a temporal scenario occurs at least once; confirms interesting states/corners are reachable.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `cover property` records whether a temporal scenario ever happens. In simulation it measures functional coverage of corner cases; in formal it proves reachability (and gives a witness trace). It also exposes vacuous assertions.

```systemverilog
// back-to-back writes with backpressure in between
c_b2b_bp: cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (valid && ready) ##1 (valid && !ready)[*2:5] ##1 (valid && ready));

// FIFO reaches full then empty
c_full_empty: cover property (@(posedge clk) full ##[1:$] empty);
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "valid", "wave": "01.....0"}, {"name": "ready", "wave": "010..10."}, {"name": "c_b2b_bp hit", "wave": "0.....10"}], "head": {"text": "the cover fires when the whole sequence matches"}}
```

### Explanation
- Assert = must always hold; cover = must happen at least once.
- Pair every important assertion with a cover of its antecedent to prove it is not vacuously passing.
- Cover results appear in the coverage database alongside covergroups.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An unreachable cover in formal means either a design bug or over-constrained assumptions.

### Follow-ups
- *cover sequence vs cover property?* `cover sequence` counts every match (including multiple per attempt).

questions.title: assume vs assert in formal verification?
questions.answer: Assertions describe what design must satisfy; assumptions constrain the environment. Over-constraining can mask bugs.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `assert` states what the design must guarantee (the tool tries to find a counterexample); `assume` restricts the inputs/environment to legal behavior (the tool only explores traces satisfying it). Over-constraining assumptions can make a buggy design pass, so assumptions must be reviewed and ideally checked as assertions on the neighboring block.

```systemverilog
// environment rule: master never drops valid without handshake
m_valid_hold: assume property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(data));

// DUT obligation
a_no_overflow: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  full |-> !wr_accept);

// sanity: make sure assumptions don't kill interesting traces
c_full: cover property (@(posedge clk) full);
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ENV["assume: legal inputs"] --> DUT["DUT"]
  DUT --> CHK["assert: required behavior"]
  ENV -. "assume at block level" .-> PEER["assert at neighbor / system level (assume-guarantee)"]
```

### Explanation
- In simulation, an `assume` is checked like an assertion (input violations reported).
- Assume-guarantee: an assumption on block B's inputs becomes an assertion on block A's outputs.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `assume property (0)` or contradictory assumptions make every assertion trivially proven; formal tools report 'over-constrained' / unreachable covers.

### Follow-ups
- *restrict property?* Constrains formal like assume but is not checked in simulation.

questions.title: What is formal equivalence checking?
questions.answer: Formal equivalence checks two versions produce equivalent behavior under assumptions; proves over huge state spaces.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Equivalence checking (LEC) proves that two designs (e.g. RTL vs synthesized netlist, or RTL before/after a refactor) produce identical outputs for all inputs, by matching state points and comparing the combinational logic cones between them. It is exhaustive, unlike simulation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  REF["reference (RTL)"] --> MAP["map key points: flops, latches, ports"]
  IMP["implementation (netlist)"] --> MAP
  MAP --> CMP["compare logic cones (SAT / BDD)"]
  CMP -->|equal| PASS["equivalent"]
  CMP -->|counterexample| FAIL["non-equivalent point + vector"]
```

| Type | Compares | Example tools / use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Combinational (LEC) | 1:1 mapped flops | RTL vs netlist after synthesis, ECO, scan insertion |
| Sequential (SEC) | designs with different state encoding/retiming | clock gating, pipelining changes |

### Explanation
- LEC runs after synthesis, DFT insertion, place & route and every ECO.
- Constraints (e.g. scan mode = 0) are needed so test logic doesn't create false differences.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- LEC proves equivalence, not correctness: a bug in RTL is faithfully reproduced in the netlist.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not just GLS?* LEC is exhaustive and much faster; GLS is for timing, X, reset behavior.

questions.title: What do lint and CDC tools check?
questions.answer: Lint finds coding/structural issues; CDC tools analyze crossings for sync/handshake/FIFO/reconvergence; neither replaces simulation/STA.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Lint finds structural/coding problems statically (width mismatches, latches, multiple drivers, unused signals, risky constructs). CDC tools find unsafe clock-domain crossings (missing synchronizers, multi-bit crossings, reconvergence, glitchy logic before sync). Both complement simulation and STA; neither proves functionality.

| Tool | Typical findings |
| --- | --- |
| Lint (Spyglass, Ascent, Verilator --lint) | width mismatch, inferred latch, multi-driver, incomplete case, unused/undriven, combinational loop, blocking in seq |
| CDC (Spyglass CDC, Questa CDC, Meridian) | unsynchronized crossing, multi-bit bus without protocol, reconvergence, combinational logic before synchronizer, reset crossings |
| RDC | async reset domain crossings causing metastability on reset assertion |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  RTL["RTL"] --> LINT["Lint"] --> CDC["CDC / RDC"] --> SIM["Simulation + assertions"] --> SYN["Synthesis"] --> STA["STA"]
```

### Explanation
- Run lint at every commit; it is cheap and catches bugs before simulation.
- CDC requires clock/reset constraints (SDC-like) to know which domains exist.
- Waivers must be reviewed: a blanket waiver hides real problems.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- CDC structural checks pass even if the protocol (e.g. holding data stable) is violated; add assertions for that.

### Follow-ups
- *How is CDC verified functionally?* Metastability injection in simulation and formal CDC protocol checks.

questions.title: What is CDC reconvergence and why is it a problem?
questions.answer: Separately synchronized related signals reconverge and settle on different cycles, creating transient wrong combinations; use a coherent protocol.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** When related signals are synchronized separately and then combined in the destination domain, their synchronizers can resolve on different cycles, so the combination briefly shows a state that never existed in the source domain.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["a (src)"] --> SA["2FF sync"] --> AND["a_s AND NOT b_s"]
  B["b (src)"] --> SB["2FF sync"] --> AND
  AND --> FSM["dst logic sees bogus pulse"]
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_dst", "wave": "p......"}, {"name": "a, b (src, change together)", "wave": "0.1...."}, {"name": "a_s", "wave": "0..1..."}, {"name": "b_s (one cycle later)", "wave": "0...1.."}, {"name": "a_s & !b_s", "wave": "0..10.."}], "head": {"text": "a and b rise together in the source; destination sees a glitch pulse"}}
```

### Explanation
- Fix: synchronize one combined/encoded signal (e.g. Gray-coded state, or a single 'valid' that qualifies a stable bus) instead of separate bits.
- Divergence-reconvergence also happens when one synchronized signal fans out to several synchronizers.
- CDC tools flag reconvergence; functional simulation needs metastability injection to expose it.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reconvergence through sequential logic (after a few flops) is also flagged and still dangerous.

### Follow-ups
- *When is it acceptable?* When the combined signals are Gray-coded (only one changes at a time).

questions.title: How should an asynchronous reset be handled across clock domains?
questions.answer: Reset is CDC-like; assertion may be async, deassertion synchronized independently per domain.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Treat reset as a crossing: assert asynchronously everywhere, but synchronize deassertion separately in each destination clock domain with its own reset synchronizer, and sequence releases if domains depend on each other.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  POR["por_n (async)"] --> RS1["rst_sync clkA"] --> DA["domain A flops"]
  POR --> RS2["rst_sync clkB"] --> DB["domain B flops"]
  POR --> RS3["rst_sync clkC"] --> DC["domain C flops"]
```

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "por_n", "wave": "0..1........"}, {"name": "clkA", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rstA_n", "wave": "0....1......"}, {"name": "clkB (slow)", "wave": "h.l.h.l.h.l."}, {"name": "rstB_n", "wave": "0.......1..."}], "head": {"text": "each domain leaves reset aligned to its own clock"}}
```

### Explanation
- Reset Domain Crossing (RDC): if a flop in reset domain R1 is reset asynchronously while it drives a flop in domain R2 that is not being reset, R2 can capture a metastable value. Fix with isolation/synchronization or by gating the receiving enable during reset.
- Different domains leave reset at different times: handshake signals must be robust to that (e.g. receivers ignore inputs until ready).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using one synchronized reset (from clkA) in clkB is itself an unsynchronized crossing.

### Follow-ups
- *What about warm resets in only one domain?* That's the classic RDC scenario.

questions.title: What determines synchronizer MTBF?
questions.answer: MTBF depends on destination frequency, data toggle rate, settling time and technology metastability parameters; extra stages improve it exponentially.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** MTBF = e^(t_r / tau) / (T_0 x f_clk x f_data): it falls with destination clock frequency and data toggle rate, and grows exponentially with the resolution time t_r (slack available for settling) relative to the flop's time constant tau. Adding a stage adds about one clock period to t_r.

| Parameter | Effect on MTBF |
| --- | --- |
| f_clk (destination) up | down (less t_r, more samples) |
| f_data up | down (more chances) |
| t_r up (extra stage, less logic between flops) | exponentially up |
| tau down (better sync cell) | exponentially up |

| Example: tau = 20 ps, T_0 = 50 ps, f_clk = 1 GHz, f_data = 100 MHz | MTBF |
| --- | --- |
| t_r = 0.5 ns (2FF with routing) | e^25 / 5e6 = 1.4e4 s (about 4 hours) |
| t_r = 1.5 ns (3FF) | e^75 / 5e6 = 7e25 s |

### Explanation
- Numbers above are illustrative; real tau/T_0 come from the library characterization.
- Each extra nanosecond of t_r multiplies MTBF by e^(1ns/tau): huge.
- System MTBF = 1 / sum(1/MTBF_i) over all synchronizers in the chip.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Logic between the two synchronizer flops eats t_r; keep them adjacent with nothing in between.

### Follow-ups
- *Target?* Typically thousands of years per synchronizer, more for automotive/medical.

questions.title: How do you pass a counter value across clock domains?
questions.answer: Binary counters change multiple bits; use Gray-coded counters for monotonically changing counts crossing domains.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A binary counter can flip many bits at once (0111 -> 1000), so direct synchronization can capture garbage. Convert to Gray code in the source domain (registered), synchronize the Gray value with 2FF, and convert back to binary in the destination.

```systemverilog
// source domain
always_ff @(posedge clk_s) begin
  cnt_bin  <= cnt_bin + inc;
  cnt_gray <= (cnt_bin + inc) ^ ((cnt_bin + inc) >> 1);   // registered Gray
end
// destination domain
always_ff @(posedge clk_d) {g2, g1} <= {g1, cnt_gray};
always_comb for (int i = 0; i < W; i++) cnt_d_bin[i] = ^(g2 >> i);  // gray2bin
```

| Binary transition | bits changing | Gray transition | bits changing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0111 -> 1000 | 4 | 0100 -> 1100 | 1 |
| 0011 -> 0100 | 3 | 0010 -> 0110 | 1 |

### Explanation
- Requirement: counter changes by at most 1 per source clock, and the destination may see it 1-2 cycles late (value is stale but valid).
- For arbitrary jumps, use a handshake that holds the value stable while it is sampled.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Generating Gray combinationally from binary right before the synchronizer can glitch; register it.

### Follow-ups
- *Fast source, slow destination?* Gray still works; the destination may skip values but never sees invalid ones.

questions.title: Explain the ready/valid handshake.
questions.answer: Transfer on clock edge when valid and ready high; producer holds valid/data stable while ready=0.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The producer asserts `valid` with data; the consumer asserts `ready` when it can accept; a transfer happens on every rising clock edge where `valid && ready`. Once valid is high, the producer must hold valid and data stable until the transfer; valid must not depend combinationally on ready.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p........"}, {"name": "valid", "wave": "01...0.1."}, {"name": "ready", "wave": "0.0.1...1"}, {"name": "data", "wave": "x=...x.=.", "data": ["D0", "D1"]}, {"name": "transfer", "wave": "0...10..1"}], "head": {"text": "D0 waits under backpressure, transfers when ready rises; D1 transfers immediately"}}
```

```systemverilog
// protocol checks
a_hold:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
            valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(data));
a_no_x:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid |-> !$isunknown(data));
```

### Explanation
- Decouples producer and consumer timing; both can stall.
- Ready may wait for valid (AXI allows that); valid must never wait for ready, or the two can deadlock.
- Throughput is one transfer per cycle when both stay high.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Dropping valid before ready (retracting) violates AXI-style protocols.

### Follow-ups
- *How to break the combinational ready path?* Skid buffer / register slice.

questions.title: What is backpressure and how must upstream logic handle it?
questions.answer: Downstream deasserts ready; upstream must hold the item until transfer; changing data while valid violates protocol.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Backpressure is the downstream deasserting `ready` because it cannot accept data. The upstream must keep the current item (valid and data unchanged) until the handshake completes, and stall or buffer any new items behind it.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk", "wave": "p........"}, {"name": "valid", "wave": "01......0"}, {"name": "ready", "wave": "1.0..1..."}, {"name": "data", "wave": "x==..===x", "data": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]}, {"name": "accepted", "wave": "x=...===x", "data": ["A", "B", "C", "D"]}], "head": {"text": "B is held for 3 cycles of backpressure, then C and D flow"}}
```

```systemverilog
// upstream stage with stall
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n)                  out_valid <= 1'b0;
  else if (!out_valid || out_ready) begin   // load only when empty or transferring
    out_valid <= in_valid;
    out_data  <= in_data;
  end
assign in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready;  // propagate backpressure
```

### Explanation
- `in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready` is the standard pipeline stage; it propagates ready combinationally back through stages (timing concern for long pipelines).
- Data loss bug: overwriting `out_data` while `out_valid && !out_ready`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Testbenches must randomize ready (including long stalls) to exercise backpressure.

### Follow-ups
- *Verification?* Assert data stability under backpressure; scoreboard order checking.

questions.title: Design a skid buffer for a ready/valid interface.
questions.answer: Small elastic buffer that breaks timing paths while preserving ready/valid; absorbs a transfer when downstream ready changes late.

questions.title: How do combinational ready/valid loops form, and how do you break them?
questions.answer: Combinational ready backward + valid forward can loop across modules; break with registered signals or skid buffer.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** If block A's valid depends combinationally on its ready input and block B's ready depends combinationally on its valid input, connecting them creates a combinational loop across the module boundary. Break it by registering one direction (skid buffer/register slice) and by never making valid depend on ready.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["block A: valid = f(ready)"] -->|valid| B["block B: ready = g(valid)"]
  B -->|ready| A
```

| Rule | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| valid must not depend combinationally on ready | removes the loop by protocol (AXI rule) |
| insert register slice / skid buffer | breaks long ready paths for timing |
| document combinational paths in interface spec | integration-time visibility |

### Explanation
- Even without a true loop, a long combinational ready chain through many stages limits frequency.
- Lint across hierarchy (or synthesis) reports the loop; simulation may hang in delta cycles.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- 'ready depends on valid' is allowed by AXI; 'valid depends on ready' is not. Both together = loop.

### Follow-ups
- *Where to place slices?* At block or subsystem boundaries and long wires.

questions.title: How do you design a parameterized SystemVerilog interface?
questions.answer: Interfaces bundle signals with modports for directional views; parameters customize widths/options for reuse.

questions.title: What is a modport?
questions.answer: A modport defines how a module views interface signals, making directions explicit and checkable.

questions.title: What is a SystemVerilog package and why use it?
questions.answer: A package stores shared types, parameters, functions and classes for reuse and consistency.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A package is a named scope holding shared types, parameters, functions, tasks, classes and covergroups, imported by modules, interfaces and other packages. It gives one typed definition instead of duplicated `include text.

```systemverilog
package bus_pkg;
  parameter int AW = 32;
  typedef enum logic [1:0] {READ, WRITE, IDLE} op_e;
  typedef struct packed { op_e op; logic [AW-1:0] addr; } req_t;
  function automatic logic parity(input logic [AW-1:0] a); return ^a; endfunction
endpackage

module dut import bus_pkg::*; (input req_t req, output logic p);
  assign p = parity(req.addr);
endmodule
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  PKG["bus_pkg"] --> DUT["dut"]
  PKG --> TB["tb / UVM env"]
  PKG --> IF["interface"]
```

### Explanation
- `import pkg::*` makes names visible on demand; `pkg::name` is explicit.
- Packages must be compiled before files that use them.
- Packages cannot contain module instances or hierarchical references.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Wildcard imports from two packages with the same name cause ambiguity errors only when the name is used.

### Follow-ups
- *Package vs `include?* Package is a single compiled scope; `include duplicates text into each unit.

questions.title: `include vs package — what is the compilation unit issue?
questions.answer: `include is textual inclusion for macros/small declarations; packages provide scoped typed reuse. Prefer packages.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `` `include`` pastes text into the current file, so the same declarations get compiled into each unit that includes them (different types, possible collisions). A package is compiled once and imported, giving one shared, typed definition.

|  | `include | package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | text substitution | named scope, import |
| Type identity | each include creates a new type | one type everywhere |
| Collisions | names leak into $unit / module | scoped (pkg::name) |
| Use for | macros, files inside a package (UVM pattern) | types, params, classes |

```systemverilog
// typical UVM structure: classes included INTO a package
package my_agent_pkg;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  `include "uvm_macros.svh"
  `include "my_item.sv"
  `include "my_driver.sv"
endpackage

// declarations outside any module/package go into $unit (compilation-unit scope) - avoid
```

### Explanation
- Classes defined in two different scopes via `include are different types even with identical text: casting between them fails.
- `$unit` scope depends on whether the tool compiles files as one unit or separately: non-portable.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Include guards (`` `ifndef FOO_SV``) avoid double inclusion inside one unit but not across packages.

### Follow-ups
- *Why include classes into the package?* One file per class for readability, single type identity via the package.

questions.title: Macro vs parameter — when do you use each?
questions.answer: Macros are text substitution without type/scope; parameters are elaboration-time constants and safer for configuration.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A macro is preprocessor text substitution with no type or scope; a parameter is a typed elaboration-time constant scoped to a module/package that can be overridden per instance. Use parameters for hardware configuration and macros only for compile-time switches or repetitive syntax.

```systemverilog
`define WIDTH 32                     // global text, last definition wins
`define MAX(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

module m #(parameter int WIDTH = 32) (...);   // per-instance, typed
`ifdef ASSERT_ON
  a_chk: assert property (...);
`endif
endmodule
```

|  | Macro | Parameter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evaluated | preprocessing (text) | elaboration |
| Type checked | no | yes |
| Per-instance value | no (global) | yes |
| Scope | file order dependent | module/package |
| Good for | ifdef switches, UVM boilerplate | widths, depths, features |

### Explanation
- Macro arguments need parentheses to avoid precedence bugs (`` `MAX(a+1, b)``).
- Redefining a macro in another file silently changes behavior depending on compile order.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `` `define`` for widths makes it impossible to instantiate two variants of a module.

### Follow-ups
- *UVM macros?* `uvm_component_utils`, `uvm_info` — boilerplate generation is a legitimate macro use.

questions.title: Interface vs module port lists — when is an interface better?
questions.answer: Interfaces bundle signals and protocol behavior, reducing port lists; useful for standard buses and verification.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Interfaces group related signals (plus modports, assertions, clocking blocks) into one port, reducing long, error-prone port lists and enabling virtual-interface connectivity in testbenches. Plain ports are more explicit and sometimes better supported by downstream tools for simple blocks.

|  | Port list | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adding a signal | edit every module and instance | edit the interface only |
| Direction checking | per port | via modport |
| TB access | hierarchical refs | virtual interface |
| Embedded checks | no | assertions, coverage |
| Tool support | universal | most tools; some flows flatten |

```systemverilog
// before
module dma (input logic clk, rst_n, output logic awvalid, input logic awready,
            output logic [31:0] awaddr, /* ... 40 more AXI signals ... */);
// after
module dma (input logic clk, rst_n, axi_if.master m_axi);
```

### Explanation
- Interfaces shine for standard buses (AXI, APB, AHB) and verification connectivity.
- At the top level / chip boundary, plain ports are usually kept for pad and tool compatibility.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Generic interface ports (`interface bus`) without a type reduce checking; use typed ports.

### Follow-ups
- *Can an interface have ports?* Yes (e.g. clk, rst_n).

questions.title: What is a virtual interface?
questions.answer: A class-level handle to a concrete interface instance; lets drivers/monitors access DUT signals without hard-coded hierarchy.

questions.title: What is a clocking block and how does it prevent races?
questions.answer: Clocking block defines sampled/driven signals relative to a clock with skews, avoiding TB/DUT races.

questions.title: What is a program block and is it still needed?
questions.answer: Program block separates TB activity from design in scheduling; modern flows prefer clocking blocks and classes.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A `program` block runs its code in the Reactive region, separating testbench execution from design (Active) execution to avoid races, and ends simulation when all programs finish. Modern UVM environments rarely use it; classes plus clocking blocks provide the same separation.

|  | module | program |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduling region | Active | Reactive |
| Can contain always blocks | yes | no |
| Can instantiate modules | yes | no |
| Implicit $finish when done | no | yes |

```systemverilog
program automatic test (bus_if.tb bus);
  initial begin
    bus.cb.req <= 1'b1;
    ##5;
    $display("gnt=%0b", bus.cb.gnt);
  end   // simulation ends when all program initial blocks complete
endprogram
```

### Explanation
- UVM recommends running `run_test()` from a module (`tb_top`), not a program, so the UVM scheduler isn't restricted.
- Clocking blocks already move TB drives to Re-NBA and sample in Preponed.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Mixing programs with UVM can cause end-of-test surprises (program-triggered `$finish`).

### Follow-ups
- *Can a program call a module task?* Yes, but a module cannot call into a program.

questions.title: How do randomization and constraints work, and what does solve...before do?
questions.answer: Class randomization subject to constraints; describe legal scenarios without over-constraining; solve-before influences ordering.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `rand`/`randc` class members are randomized by `randomize()` subject to all active constraints; the solver picks uniformly from the *legal solution space*. `solve a before b` changes the probability distribution (not the legal set) by picking `a` first.

```systemverilog
class pkt;
  rand bit       is_small;
  rand bit [9:0] len;
  constraint c_len  { is_small -> len < 16; len > 0; }
  constraint c_ord  { solve is_small before len; }   // 50% small, not 16/1023
endclass

pkt p = new();
assert (p.randomize() with { len != 8; });           // inline constraint
p.c_ord.constraint_mode(0);                          // disable a constraint
p.is_small.rand_mode(0);                             // freeze a variable
```

| Without solve-before | With solve is_small before len |
| --- | --- |
| P(is_small=1) = 15 / (15 + 1023) ~ 1.4% | P(is_small=1) = 50% |
| uniform over all (is_small, len) pairs | is_small chosen first, then len |

### Explanation
- Good constraints describe legality; distributions (`dist`) and solve-before shape interesting stimulus.
- `pre_randomize`/`post_randomize` hooks compute derived fields.
- Always check the `randomize()` return value (failure leaves values unchanged).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Over-constraining prevents hitting corner cases; under-constraining creates illegal stimulus. `randc` variables cannot appear in solve-before.

### Follow-ups
- *Soft constraints?* `soft len == 64;` can be overridden by later constraints without failure.

questions.title: What is functional coverage and how is it different from code coverage?
questions.answer: Functional coverage measures whether intended scenarios/values/crosses were exercised; complements code coverage.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Functional coverage (covergroups, cover properties) measures whether specified scenarios, values, crosses and transitions were exercised; code coverage (line, branch, toggle, FSM, expression) measures which RTL was executed. 100% code coverage can still miss important protocol combinations.

```systemverilog
covergroup cg_pkt @(posedge clk iff valid && ready);
  cp_len:  coverpoint len  { bins small = {[1:15]}; bins mid = {[16:255]}; bins big = {[256:1023]}; }
  cp_type: coverpoint kind { bins rd = {READ}; bins wr = {WRITE}; }
  cp_bp:   coverpoint stall_cycles { bins none = {0}; bins some = {[1:3]}; bins long = {[4:$]}; }
  x_len_type: cross cp_len, cp_type;
  cp_seq:  coverpoint kind { bins wr_after_rd = (READ => WRITE); }
endgroup
```

|  | Code coverage | Functional coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | automatic from RTL | written from the verification plan |
| Answers | what code ran | what features/scenarios were tested |
| Misses | missing features, combinations | untested code (unless reviewed) |

### Explanation
- Use both: code holes reveal untested logic; functional holes reveal untested features.
- Coverage closure drives test/constraint tuning in constrained-random flows.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Coverage sampled at the wrong time (e.g. without the handshake qualifier) inflates numbers.

### Follow-ups
- *Cross explosion?* Use `ignore_bins`/`illegal_bins` and `binsof` to prune crosses.

questions.title: Describe a robust RTL verification and sign-off flow.
questions.answer: Combine spec review, coding standards, lint, CDC/RDC, simulation with directed and CR tests, assertions, coverage, formal, synthesis checks, STA, power and GLS. No single tool proves correctness.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** No single tool proves correctness; a sign-off flow layers checks that each catch a different class of risk: spec review -> lint/CDC/RDC -> simulation (directed + constrained random) with assertions and coverage -> formal where valuable -> synthesis/LEC -> STA/power -> gate-level and timing validation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  SPEC["spec review + verification plan"] --> LINT["lint, CDC, RDC"]
  LINT --> SIM["UVM simulation: directed + constrained random"]
  SIM --> ASSERT["assertions + functional/code coverage closure"]
  ASSERT --> FORMAL["formal: property, connectivity, X, unreachability"]
  FORMAL --> SYN["synthesis + LEC"]
  SYN --> STA["STA + power analysis"]
  STA --> GLS["gate-level sim with SDF, low-power sim (UPF)"]
  GLS --> SIGN["sign-off review: coverage, bug trend, waivers"]
```

| Stage | Catches |
| --- | --- |
| Lint | coding/structural errors |
| CDC/RDC | crossing and reset hazards |
| Simulation + coverage | functional bugs, untested features |
| Formal | corner cases, deadlocks, proofs |
| LEC | synthesis/ECO errors |
| STA | timing |
| GLS | X/reset/init, timing-constraint mistakes |

### Explanation
- Sign-off criteria: 100% plan items covered, code coverage reviewed with waivers, zero open critical bugs, bug-rate trend flattened, all lint/CDC waivers reviewed.
- Regressions run continuously with seeds; failures triaged daily.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Treating coverage percentage as the goal instead of verifying the plan's features.

### Follow-ups
- *When is verification done?* When sign-off criteria are met and the bug discovery rate has converged, not when tests pass.
